(223); 4 Angad Cheema, 5 Karan Vasudeva (224); 6 Samresh Sardar (227);

7 Aman Guron (228); 8 Kanishk Madan, 9 Manav Das, 10 Pawan Kumar,11 Gagan Verma (229).

Heading: Ludhiana PS set to be a model for others to follow - Indian Express
Content:
Rajni Walia of Government College for Women, Ludhiana claimed the gold medal in 44 Kg category in the Panjab University Judo Championship (Women) being held at Panjab University Gymnasium Hall on Thursday. Priya of Guru Nanak Girls College, Ludhiana grabbed the silver medal in the same category while Rupinder Kaur of Dev Samaj College for Women, Chandigarh and Yoshoda Verma of MCM DAV College for Women, Chandigarh claimed the bronze medal.

In the 48 Kg category, Sarita of GGS College for Women, Chandigarh claimed the gold medal while Bandana Devi of Guru Nanak Girls College, Ludhiana grabbed the silver medal. Heena Verma of DAV College, Chandigarh and Nidhia Sharma of MCM DAV College for Women, Chandigarh claimed the bronze medal. In the 52 Kg category Renu Kashyap of GGS College for Women, Chandigarh claimed the top spot while Sonam of Guru Nanak Girls College, Ludhiana grabbed the silver medal. Monika of Guru Nanak Khalsa College for Women, Ludhiana and Ruksana of Government College for Girls, Sector 11 grabbed the bronze medal.

Komal Saini of DAV College, Chandigarh claimed the gold medal in the 57 Kg category while Manju Devi of MCM DAV College, Chandigarh grabbed the silver medal. Kiwi of Dev Samaj College for Women and Meenu Arora of Guru Nanak Girls College, Ludhiana grabbed the bronze medal.

Heading: The focus shifts to preventing the disease - Indian Express
Content:
Sarabha Nagar police station puts a premium on beat coverage

To make policing more effective and people-friendly, the Sarabha Nagar police station is being developed as a model police station. The project is likely to become functional within a fortnight.

For the project, the entire area under the Sarabha Nagar police station has been divided into 21 beats and each beat has been assigned a beat officer. Each beat officer will have all the details about the residents and the buildings and other places in the area. These beat officers will be directly in touch with the station house officer (SHO) of the police station. Besides, these beat officers will be attached to the police control room (PCR).

Sources said that the project was aimed at improving the efficiency of the police and enabling the police to reach out to the public quickly. Sources said the beat officers have already started collecting details of their area.

Sarabha Nagar SHO Devinder Kumar said on the project has already begun and SSP R.K. Jaiswal was supervising it.

SSP Jaiswal told Newsline, "This work has been initiated on the directions of the Director General of Police (DGP), Punjab, NPS Aulakh. Similar model police stations are being developed all over the state. In Ludhiana, we have begun with Sarabha Nagar police station but later other police stations may also be developed on this pattern."

The SSP further said, "Once it is fully functional, the model police station will look like a corporate office. People will be surprised to see not only the modern furniture and other facilities here but will also find the behaviour of the police personnel friendly."

SSP Jaiswal said the model police station might start working within a fortnight.

Heading: Canadian cops visit Jagraon to get leads in Kanishka bombing case - Indian Express
Content:
As the theme of World Diabetes Day being celebrated on Friday focuses on occurrence of diabetes in children and adolescents, the medical fraternity is more concerned about knowing the preventive measures to fight the disease more effectively.

'Pregnancy with diabetes' has caught the attention of the doctors around the world and is being researched extensively.

City-based researcher Dr Geeti Puri Arora, currently working as a consultant physician and diabetologist at Deep Hospital, is one of the researchers who are part of the comprehensive project sponsored by a Swedish university. The project aims to list the factors in pregnant women that lead to occurrence of diabetes in their children.

She says the focus is now towards finding ways to prevent the disease with the help of research on 'pregnancy with diabetes.' "But pregnant women, in both rural and urban areas, are not aware enough to get themselves diagnosed to find sugar level in their bodies. This ignorance among women hinders in taking preventive steps in time," she said.

The project will include about 5,000 subjects (pregnant women) from three cities in the state – Ludhiana, Hoshiarpur and Amritsar. "We have already conducted a pilot project by screening some 100 pregnant women and found that seven of them had diabetes and 3-4 were border-line cases. Based on this, the rate of incidence of diabetes in pregnant women in the area can be said to be around 10-12 per cent."

She added: "But when we will have the data of 5,000 pregnant women along with their family history, we will be in a better position to have a comprehensive idea. We know that Type 2 diabetes is genetic but we need to know the factors causing diabetes in kids who don't have family history of the disease."

She further said that about 60-70 per cent of the people who have diabetes do not even know it before it is late and are left with less than 50 per cent of the cells to make insulin. "So timely diagnosis is very crucial," she said.

India is already tipped to be the diabetes capital of the world with largest population of diabetics in the world. At present, about 30-35 millions Indians suffer from diabetes. The population of diabetics all over the world is put at over 250 million.

Heading: Osteoporosis no longer found in women, elderly only - Indian Express
Content:
Three officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) visited Jagraon on Thursday in connection with the investigation of the 1985 bombing of Air India's Kanishka, and questioned a resident of Rasheen village.

The Canadian Police's meeting with Nahour Singh is learnt to have lasted for over 40 minutes.

Singh is not wanted by the Canadian Police directly for the bombings, but authorities believe that he could provide some leads in the case.

Incidentally, it has also been learnt that the Canadian Police have asked the Ludhiana police to look for the whereabouts of two people, namely, Karambir Singh and Mohan Singh. Mohan Singh's name appears on the list of the nine names released by the RCMP.

The RCMP team has been in Punjab to conduct investigations into the June 1985 bombing of Kanishka off the coast of Ireland and a related explosion in the transit area of Tokyo's Narita Airport in which 331 people died.

Canadian authorities believe that top Babbar Khalsa International (BKI) hitmen Jagtar Singh Hawara and Paramjit Singh Bheora, could provide significant leads to help solve the 23-year-old bombing.

The two hitmen successively led the group's terror strikes in India for several years, and are known to have been associated with Canada-based Babbar activists and sympathisers.

Christened the 'Air India Task Force', the RCMP squad have requested police authorities in Punjab, Chandigarh, Himachal Pradesh and the CBI "to locate and make available for interview" a number of other individuals who are believed to be potential witnesses.

While SSP Ludhiana R K Jaiswal refused to divulge any details, it has been learnt that Mohan Singh, who is a resident of Dhakha, died long ago in a foreign country.

At the same time, Karambir Singh, who is a resident of some area near Jodhewal, has not returned home for years. Both these men have had links with terrorist activities.

Heading: Teaching is his profession, serving society a passion - Indian Express
Content:
Osteoporosis has always been associated with women in late forties, but a recent finding gives an altogether different picture: Men are equally prone to it and 70 years is no longer the age when people generally land up in clinics with joint problems.

At the bone density camps at GTB Hospital, even men in their thirties have been found suffering from osteoporosis and the disease is highly common in 50 plus men.

Dr R S Sodhi, an orthopaedic doctor and medical superintendent at GTB Hospital said: "At the recently held camp at our hospital, we were surprised to get equal osteoporosis ratio among men and women. The change has occurred because of the change in life styles, use of drugs, alcohol and smoking. Most women suffer from this problem after the age of 45 when they go under menopause and hormonal changes happen due to that. But now the occurrence has been found among men."

Dr Harpal Singh, an orthopaedic at the DMC Hospital, said: "Even young women are also landing up with these problems which is more because of a lack of proper diet and less exposure to sunlight. Their diet fails to balance the lack of Vitamin D in their bodies. Recently, men having lack of calcium have started approaching us."

Dr H S Gill, an expert associated with SPS Apollo Hospital, said: "These days 30 per cent of my patients having osteoporosis are men and that too in their late forties or early fifties. This trend is recent and it is high time that men take care of their lifestyles. They must exercise and should often come out of their air conditioned offices.'

Doctors say that 15 minutes' exposure to sunlight in the early morning is a must to get enough vitamin D. It strengthens our bones. A good amount of calcium intake is also a must in the daily diet to avoid joint problems in the mid-thirties, say experts.

Heading: MCD faces court ire for land grab - Indian Express
Content:
A primary school teacher has devoted his life for the causes of environment and HIV positive people

He teaches at a government primary school in Dhannsu in Ludhiana district to earn his living but his passion is to take care of the environment. Besides, he has also dedicated his life to work for the cause of HIV positive people in the state.

Jagjeetsingh Maan has set up two NGOs – 'Watawaran Sambhal Society' and the 'Punjab Networking of Positive People Society.'

Maan started spreading awareness about these two issues among school children and village communities.

He says: "These NGOs are the outcome of my discussions with my colleagues. Many of the 100 members of 'Watawaran Sambhal Society' are school teachers. With the exception of me, all the 175 members of my other NGO are HIV positive."

He says he tries to devote his time to both the activities.

"Whatever free time I get after my school duty, I devote to these activities. I use even my casual leave and holidays for the purpose. My wife Manminder Kaur always cooperates with me in this social causes. I also counsel and motivate HIV positive and AIDS patients to lead a better life. We have been able to spread awareness about these diseases in more than 35 villages of Punjab," he says.

Maan says his environmental NGO has planted about 10,000 saplings by now.

He says the idea to serve people came to his mind in 2005 when one of his friends told him about an HIV positive driver in their village.

"I contacted different authorities to help the driver but he did not survive. After his death, I found that many other villagers were HIV positive. It was then that I decided to establish a common platform for these people. At present, the members of our organisation include many widows whom we support morally, financially and socially," he says.

Maan's NGO distributes nutritious food freely to needy HIV positive people every month. He says: "We accept pulses, flour, refined oil and peanuts from voluntary donors and distribute them among 20 poor patients every month."

Maan, a victim of the 1984 riots, further says: "There are many reasons for the spread of the disease. The society secludes HIV and AIDS patients from the mainstream. The government officials have an indifferent attitude towards these people and the families having HIV positive members prefer to keep things under wrap. My NGO is working hard to bring a change in society but the government officials need to change their attitude."

Heading: Dead boy’s kin accuse cops of custody death - Indian Express
Content:
A 76-year-old woman, mired in a legal wrangle with the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) for over a decade to win back the title of her land, has finally been granted lawful possession by the court.

It all began in 1991 when the civic body obtained a court order against Saroj Rani Jaggi, claiming that a 'disputed' land at New Friends Colony did not belong to her and the five-storey building erected on it was illegal.

Armed with documents that showed the land had been handed over to the MCD by the New Friends Cooperative House Building Society way back in 1978, and the same had been earmarked for the development of a public park, MCD officials managed to procure an order from an additional district judge.

The building was destroyed, and Jaggi was held "encroacher" by the court.

Aggrieved, Jaggi decided to move an appeal against the order and filed a petition claiming her right over the land. She also demanded a hold on the demolition order.

Almost four years into the hearing, when Additional District Judge (ADJ) Kamini Lau sought to verify the credibility of the document regarding the land transfer by Jaggi, representatives of the civic body produced a photocopy that seemed fudged — with a few words inserted that were not there on the original.

Demanding an explanation for the fudging, the irate judge said that it was evidently a "fabrication and an attempt to mislead" the court.

"Either they had taken a factually incorrect stand before the judge in 1991, or that they are at present not coming out with facts and the material," said ADJ Lau.

Jaggi, on the other hand, adduced the registered sale deed and other documents relating to on water tax and property tax assessments, which were found to be genuine.

ADJ Lau then accorded relief to Jaggi, who could not be present in court due to her advanced years and was represented by her husband, and passed a decree declaring her to be the owner of the land. However, the court refused to hold the demolition order as illegal, after she failed to produce evidence sanctioning the construction.

Heading: Fiscal brake hits canvas but artists hopeful - Indian Express
Content:
Relatives of an 18-year-old boy have levelled allegations of custodial death against officers of the Nihal Vihar Police Station in West Delhi. Police, however, said the boy was lynched by locals after he was caught stealing in the area.

The deceased, Gaurav Singh, a resident of Shiv Ram Park in Nilotti had gone out with his friend Deepak on Wednesday night. When he did not return for a long time, his parents got worried and started looking for him without success.

"On Thursday morning, some police officers called and told me that my son was dead. I went with a few relatives to the Nihal Vihar Police Station. My son was caught stealing by the police and brought to the police station. He was then allegedly thrashed to death," Gaurav's father, Mahender Singh alleged.

Deputy Commissioner of Police (West) Sharad Aggarwal, however denied the charges and said that locals had beaten up the boy after he was caught stealing.

"We got a PCR call around 5 am on Thursday. The residents of Nihal Vihar handed the boy over to the PCR and claimed he was caught stealing. Police rushed the boy to the Sanjay Gandhi Hospital where he died during treatment. His relatives were then informed about the incident," DCP Aggarwal said.

Police said a murder case has been registered against unknown people and locals are being questioned regarding the boy's death. Gaurav's body has been transferred to the Sanjay Gandhi Mortuary, police added.

Gaurav's father, Mahender Singh, runs a weekly bazaar in the area, while Gaurav was unemployed.

Heading: Constable hangs self in New Ashok Nagar - Indian Express
Content:
After returning with unsold tags at the Sotheby's Hong Kong auction last month, Subodh Gupta and Justin Ponmany's canvases bagged bids galore when they went under the hammer in Delhi, under the Saffronart banner, on Tuesday and Wednesday.

But there's a specific reason behind the impressive show: it was a charitable auction.

Organised by city-based artist couple Subodh Gupta and Bharti Kher to gather funds for Orissa and Bihar flood victims, proceeds from the auction will be directed to the NGOs Samajik Shaikshanik Vikas Kendra and Goonj. While the former will use funds to provide basic amenities such as clothes and food to the victims, Goonj will use it to build homes.

"But the global financial crisis has resulted in the emergence of a collectors' market rather than an investors' market," says Dinesh Vazirani, founder of Saffronart.

Gupta's canvas from the utensil series managed to garner an impressive Rs 1.70 crore, while Ponmany's pen-and-ink paperwork sold for over a lakh.

"The result proves that quality artwork is still selling," Vazirani says. "We had bids coming from the world over, including the US and Europe." He says the results recorded a sale of Rs 3.93 crore, with 22 of the 31 canvases finding buyers.

Tripat Kalra, director of Gallerie Nvya in Delhi did not participate in the auction but the result instills hope that her exhibition 'Dus Mahavidyas', which began at Visual Arts Gallery on Wednesday, will also interest collectors. Comprising work by 10 women artists, including Shobha Broota and Arpana Caur, Kalra has been working towards the show for a year. "We received a phenomenal response during the opening," Kalra says. "There isn't really an art recession but the slump is affecting art."

Sunaina Anand, director of Art Alive gallery, agrees. Not many in the art mart are taking the risk of introducing younger artists in the circuit but Anand is going ahead with a solo of Santiniketan-based Manjari Charkravarti. She does, however, admit that Delhi has not remained unaffected by the slowdown. "If we were selling an approximate 10 canvases a month till May, the figure has dipped to three now," she says. "The drop in prices has been observed with the work of contemporary artists whose price had unnaturally risen."

Till recently her gallery had on display artwork by Paris-based artist Sakti Burman. Priced between Rs 8 lakh to Rs 80 lakh, Anand managed a sales figure of 40 per cent. "That is very good in the current scenario," she beams.

Heading: Call centre cab overturns in Dwarka: 1 killed, 5 injured - Indian Express
Content:
Go baby
Purav Bhandare sure is on a roll. The eight-year-old actor, who started his career in the public eye at just four, is in talks with UK film director Steve Barron for a role in his yet-untitled film. Barron, who's best known for his cult comedy, 1993's Coneheads, was looking for a young face and Santosh Sivan, who'd worked with young Purav in Tahaan, recommended him. The young actor has already auditioned for the role and is now just awaiting the final call for formalities.

International calling card
Cat-eyed beauty Celina Jaitley does not believe in resting on her laurels. After the amazing response her latest Bollywood venture, Golmaal Returns, got at the box office, Celina is now set to woo the international audience with her first international film Love Has No Language. She was recently spotted at the movie's premiere in Auckland, New Zealand, along with her Australian co-star, Ben Mitchell and New Zealand rugby star Monty Beetham. The Kiwi rugger was apparently quite taken with Celina's beauty and the lovely lass herself was floored by all the warmth and attention she received.

Shining star
Divya Dutta's prospects in films have never been better. She started out on the idiot box, and graduated to small but significant roles in movies like Veer-Zaara and has now finally landed herself the lead role in Zee Limelight's first presentation Oh My God!! She's acting with Vinay Pathak, Saurabh Shukla, and Harsh Chhaya in the movie, which is about a simple man, who with god's help, comes to term with his big dreams and his journey thereafter. Divya even appeared as a celebrity judge on Sony Television's hit comedy show Comedy Circus - Kaante ki Takkar to promote her movie which will release on December 5 this year.

Heading: Madrid Beckons - Indian Express
Content:
As the Tranoi Fair celebrates India in its autumn-winter edition, designer Abhishek Dutta gets a surprise invite

While he was prepping the models and giving last-minute tucks for his comeback show at the Wills Lifestyle India Fashion Week last month, designer Abhishek Dutta (inset) had little inkling that someone in the audience already had big plans for him. "I saw Michael Hadida, the owner of the prestigious Tranoi Fair, in the front row and was happy, particularly because he had earlier come to my stall and browsed through the clothes. But I was so busy ensuring everything went off without a hitch that I didn't think anything beyond that," says Dutta.

It was his return to the Delhi fashion week, after four consecutive showings at the Lakme Fashion Week in Mumbai. Now, Dutta can book another ticket — to Paris and its prestigious Tranoi Fair.

Dutta's collection — a series of quirky outfits that included zippered cargos, khadi jackets, shorts and capris and dresses with appliqués, all in linen and cotton — subtly played up the Indian theme on overtly western silhouettes, and won him accolades from fashionistas. Much later, the designer from Kolkata came to know that Hadida had included him and newbie designer duo Nidhi and Pankaj for the autumn-winter edition of the fair, scheduled to take off in Paris between March 2 and 5 next year.

Incidentally, Tranoi is celebrating India as its theme at this year's fair, with an India Pavilion showcasing the works of over 15 of India's top designers. "I first heard the news from the media, but it was only when there was a correspondence from Hadida's office that I was convinced that I was actually going," laughs 29-year-old Dutta, who launched his pret label, Adnormal, in 2004, and now supplies to over 20 stores across the country, including Kimaya and Azara.

While the designer is busy working on the orders that he has received after the fashion week, his blueprint for Tranoi is also ready. "I am not much into bling since it's only suited to the Indian context. I am working towards developing new fabrics and reviving old weaving techniques, so that my Indian sensibilities come across even on a western silhouette," says Dutta, who counts actors Vidya Balan, Salman Khan, Abhishek Bachchan, and Raima and Riya Sen among his clients.

Heading: QUEST -  A schools’ initiative from The Indian Express - Indian Express
Content:
When the Contemporary Art (ARCO) fair opens in Madrid on February 11, India will be on display as the guest country. The director of ARCO, Lourdes Fernández, announced in Delhi that there would be a special section, Panorama for India, which would be curated by artist Bose Krishnamachari. "We have always been open to emerging art," said Fernandez. While South Korea was the guest country in 2007, it was Brazil in 2008. Fernández said she liked the works of Jitish Kallat and Shilpa Gupta, though she had yet to go deep into Indian art.

"It is a great opportunity for India and the Indian panorama has around 9,000 square feet to showcase the works," said Krishnamachari. There will be 13 Indian galleries, including Bodhi Art, Chemould Prescott, Gallery Espace and Nature Morte. There will also be a separate space for Bose to showcase a few of his favourite artists, like Ravinder Reddy and Riyas Komu. Apart from Indian galleries, there will be over 250 galleries from around the world, with 79 from Spain.

But with the market meltdown, even the Frieze Art Fair in London had seen a dip in the sales. No stranger to the economic crisis, Fernandez said, "The economic meltdown has touched us all but we are in the same position as other fairs such as Miami and Basel." Warding off fears of a lukewarm response, Krishnamachari said, "Keeping this in mind, we have suggested a limited number of artists to the galleries, with a mix of new talent and established names to balance the show." Let's wait for the Spanish show.

Heading: What draws out Delhi? - Indian Express
Content:
"With the elephant of communalism roaming around untamed after attacks against minorities, I am like a mahout who can tame it, but for that I require a whip, which you can give me in the form of the Jamia Nagar assembly seat," — Amar Singh, general secretary, Samajwadi party

In 2003, Tilak Nagar, Tri Nagar and Krishna Nagar saw the highest voter turn out. Sobhana K finds out the why and how

Tilak Nagar
(60.45% polling in 2003)
The deafening sounds of drums and chants reverberate through Tilak Nagar, as residents celebrate Guru Nanak Jayanti. People follow the procession, distributing sweets. The constituency votes with almost a similar fervour as well. In the past three Assembly polls, the number of votes has exceeded 54,000 each year; in 2003 this number shot up to 62,153.

"I have never missed a single election, neither have my family and friends," Ranjeet Singh, a shopkeeper in Sant Nagar, says. The vote base here is unified and politically active. Thirty-four per cent of the population is Sikh, while 25 per cent are Punjabi. Although no big hoardings introducing candidates can be seen, the awareness levels among voters are high. Most residents easily recognise their candidates.

The area MLAs hop from one gurudwara procession, registering their presence, to another, in an effort to cover as many places as possible. "I have been out since 5 am and the public meetings will continue till 10," two times BJP MLA O P Babbar (70), who walks barefoot behind the procession, says.

Just a few metres away, his Congress opponent, Anita Babbar, is also busy campaigning. Public meetings started here much ahead of any where else.

Tri Nagar
(60% polling in 2003)
Largely an industrial hub, the area will witness a close BJP and Congress fight. Block level workers of both parties are very active here.

A majority among the 1.46 lakh voters live in resettlement colonies and JJ clusters. There are only 35 group housing societies in this constituency. Politicians in the area, meanwhile, believe that the reason for a high turnout is the direct clash between the Congress and the BJP. In the last Assembly elections held in 2003, the number of votes increased by nearly 7,000, when compared to 1998. "No third party has ever played any role here. It has always been a ground for a close contest between the BJP and the Congress, which brings most voters out," BJP candidate and two-time MLA from the area Nand Kishore Garg said.

Garg won the seat in 1993 and 1998 but lost in the last elections to Congress candidate Anil Bhardwaj. Surrounded by sea of marigold flowers, as Garg goes door-to-door, campaigning in the unauthorised Raja Park colony of his constituency, just a few blocks away in Shakurpur village, his opponent is meeting RWA heads of the area in a house.

"There are six people in our house who are eligible for voting, so we definitely want to know who is standing for election. The present MLA claims he has done a lot of developmental work in the area. But roads in our colonies have still not been constructed," Kusum Tiwari, a resident, said.

Krishna Nagar
(61.3% polling in 2003)
The Delhi BJP chief, Harsh Vardhan, has won the last three Assembly elections from this area. It has a sizeable middle class population, which goes to vote without any caste or party bias in mind. "My motto has always been to have a personal touch with each voter. So, during each election, I try to reach out to every door and say hello to every one," Harsh Vardhan said as he walked from door to door in New Govind Pura, greeting each voter.

It's a predominantly Punjabi and Jain population. After delimitation, a part of the Geeta Colony constituency, which has a sizeable Muslim population, has also been added to this constituency.

Political pundits claim that the only reason for the high turnout here is that one of the BJP's "heavy weights" is contesting the elections here. "The BJP has campaigned hard for nearly a month here, ahead of the elections," a Congress worker said. The vote count here increased by 5,000 in the last Assembly elections.

The Congress has fielded Deepika Khullar from the area.

Heading: VOTERS SPEAK: Chander Tiwari - Indian Express
Content:
Standing councillors of the Congress, Akali Dal, Bahujan Samajwadi Party (BSP) and the Lok Janshakti Party (LJP) have had better luck than BJP councillors.

While the BJP remained firm and did not give tickets to any of its standing councillors, 19 councillors from different parties have filed their nominations to contest the Assembly elections later this month.

Eight councillors from the Congress, three from the Akali Dal, BSP and LJP each, and one each from the NCP and Indian National Lok Dal will be contesting the elections. They will be contesting the Assembly elections for the first time. Twelve of these 19 will be contesting against the standing MLA of the area.

Councillor Umed Iqbal of the LJP will contest against Congress standing MLA Haroon Yusuf from the Ballimaran Assembly seat. Congress councillor Anita Babbar will be contesting against O P Babbar, the undefeated MLA from Tilak Nagar for the past eight terms. And Deepika Khullar of the Congress will contest against Harsh Vardhan of the BJP from Krishna Nagar.

Two councillors who were refused tickets from their party joined other parties to contest the elections. Congress councillor Satbir Singh, who was refused a ticket from Mehrauli, will be contesting as an independent candidate from the area. Duli Chand Lohia, who was refused a ticket by the Congress, has joined the NCP to contest from Rajouri Garden.

Independent councillor Nand Kishore of Najafgarh has been given a ticket by the Congress to contest from Vikaspuri. Three BSP councillors, Sharad Chauhan, Satpal and Sahi Ram, have got tickets to contest from Assembly constituencies that fall in their Municipal wards. Councillor Duli Chand Lohia and Avtar Singh Hit will once again see each other at Rajouri Garden.

Heading: DPCC appoints poll observers for all 70 constituencies - Indian Express
Content:
Not so funny
Move over Modi, L K Advani and other big BJP guns. Now is the time for the hasya kavi to campaign for the BJP. The only problem the BJP is, however, facing is who will pay the bill of these humourists. Serious discussions were held till late night on whether funds would come from the central body or whether candidates would pay themselves for these humourists. Nothing funny about this it seems.

SP taps into Muslim sentiments
The Samajwadi Party on Thursday chose to tap Muslim sentiments post -Batla House encounter and called upon the community to empower the party in order to curb communal forces. SP general secretary Amar Singh addressed a gathering of Jamia Millia Islamia students and members of the minority community. Singh said the SP is the "hand" of the community — "And you have the might to empower us, you are my force. So on the day of voting, whomsoever you feel has been a true sympathiser, vote for the representative of that party".

Heading: JNU prof moves minority panel - Indian Express
Content:
The Delhi Congress appointed election observers for all 70 Assembly constituencies in the Capital on Thursday.

Delhi Pradesh Congress Committee (DPCC) president Jai Prakash Aggarwal said each constituency will have one constituency observer and a PCC observer.

While the constituency observer will be confined to the assigned constituency, the PCC observer will have jurisdiction over four to five constituencies.

The party today announced the names of 83 party workers, which included 70 constituency observers and 14 PCC observers.

Heading: All FMS students book a berth for summer internships - Indian Express
Content:
The National Commission for Minorities has issued a notice to Jawaharlal Nehru University regarding alleged discrimination by the university in considering a candidate for the post of associate professor.

The letter, of which Newsline has a copy, has asked the university to look into the matter and has sought an explanation.

In a letter written to the NCM on October 25, Dr Akhlaque Ahmad Ansari, an assistant professor at JNU, said his name along with 11 others was listed for promotion. But, while JNU appointed 95 people teaching positions in July and took in the other 11, only he was left out. Ansari said he was the only candidate belonging to the minority community.

"The support and favouritism of university authorities on personal grounds is harming the academic environment in the university and particularly in the Centre. Besides, I am aggrieved and feel discriminated against, and due to this hostile situation, I am under immense mental stress and depression," Ansari said in his letter.

Heading: writ right, but just missed the target! - Indian Express
Content:
Stipends register a 21 per cent rise

In what are being reported as the best summer internship deals of all times, students at the Faculty of Management Studies have clinched internships with top MNCs, among them American companies. Stipends have registered a 21 per cent hike and, in the biggest deal, a student will earn Rs1 lakh for two months.

With multiple offers being made by companies to students of the two full-time programmes: 107 in MBA and 48 in MBA-MS, the average stipend this year rose to Rs 37,000 per month from last year's Rs 29,000. Also, while last year 73 companies came for recruitments, this time the number has risen to 93.

Students said the substantial hikes in stipends were possible because the global slowdown has affected the finance and banking sector; but fast moving consumer goods (FMCG) have not felt the impact. "As most of the placements have been done in companies dealing with consumer goods, such as P&G, Coca Cola, Cadbury, ITC, Perfetti, Colgate Palmolive and Nestle etc, we got good bargains," Sriharsha K R S A, a member of the college media committee, said.

Companies will also give a lot of perks to the students in the form of credit cards and other allowances. Sukhbir Chimni, a student who has been recruited by Proctor and Gamble, however, said that more than the money, it's the experience that matters for most students. "There will be a lot of work, as I will be sent to Mumbai and from there to rural areas. Nothing will come easy," he said.

Summer internships are part of the academic curriculum of MBA first year, where every student has to intern with a company for a minimum of two months. The internships begin in April and depending on progress made, can sometimes extend to three or four months as well.

The placement convener, Professor Madhu Vij, said: "Summer internships are critical for providing students with the much needed corporate exposure. The record 100 per cent summer placements this year, despite the global financial meltdown and general downturn in the industry, reaffirm the premier stature this campus enjoys."

Heading: Children from Vikaspuri slum have a ball with students of St Mark’s - Indian Express
Content:
The successful maneuvre on November 8 that put Chandrayyan-I in an orbit around the moon, marked the completion of the most important phase of the Indian lunar mission.

Although ISRO's inherent scientific ability was never in doubt, Chandrayaan-I, India's maiden deep space endeavour achieved new technological challenges in telemetry, tracking, miniaturisation of devices and other challenges that were hitherto not experienced in the near-earth environment. The performance of the mission so far is testimony to ISRO's advanced capabilities in all these respects. Neverthless, as ISRO plans for Chandrayaan-II in 2012-13 and a manned mission to space in 2015, when it will face even greater technology challenges.

A political factor that is relevant is the world's constant India -China comparison and the latter's demonstrated technological prowess in space technology. Given the resurgent interest in tapping the moon's resources, there is a strategic dimension to space missions as well. This becomes particularly relevant if one notes the discordance between the Moon Treaty, which very few countries have signed and ratified and the Outer Space Treaty, which most nations have. While the former emphasises the principle of the common heritage of mankind; the latter articulates it weakly. It is from this perceptive that the rhetorical question posed by ISRO's former chairman K Kasturirangan needs to be viewed, "Can we afford not to go to moon?" and the basic question of whether India should venture into deep space be addressed. At the same time, as ISRO begins to think in terms of manned mission to space, cost-benefit analyses need to be done more rigorously than for relatively low-cost missions to space, such as the Chandrayaan. But these are policy issues that can be taken up later. Now is the time to congratulate ISRO on taking India's exploration of space up a level-which very few developing countries have even aspired to reach.
- Ashuthosh Yadav, XI-A, Bharti Public School, Mayur Vihar

Picture this. A day before her Class XII Boards exams, Shilpa is brushing up her concepts and incessantly muttering some formula or the other. At night, she is really nervous about her exam, and her mother comforts her and puts her to bed at 1 in the night with a promise to wake her up at 5 in morning .Shilpa gets up at dawn after a sleepless night spent tossing from one side to the other. She sits once again with her Maths books. Feeling as if she has forgotten everything, she starts getting worried and panicky. With her mind occupied with formulas, she brushes her teeth and gets ready to go to the disignated exam centre. Her mother gives her a glass of milk to drink and breakfast, but she refuses, saying she would puke everything out if she eats. Then she goes to the temple and prays, after which her parents drop her off at the examination centre.

This is a common scenario which each one of us goes through at some point or the other in our lives.

With the Indian education system judging the intelligence of a person in the span merely three hours, a student's life is often made extremely miserable.

In my view three hours are too few to judge the potential and capability of a student, especially if a student is taken ill in those three hours. The education system requires us to mug up and reproduce everything during exam hours word by word, sentence by sentence. It id unfirtunate that our education system is not producing the next batch of achievers but the next line of crammers.

History is proof that all great men who made a mark for themselves were not the ones who crammed information but were the ones who thought out of the box and had the guts to do things that others would not have thought of.

Look at Albert Einstein, who never liked history because it required learning the dates by heart. The result, however, is before all of us — he was one of the most intelligent and famous scientists of all time.

Our education system needs to change to produce great results.
- Divya Mahajan, XII-C, Ramjas school, Pusa Road

Heading: Rail trail - Indian Express
Content:
A large group of children from the Vikaspuri slum gather every day in a small room to learn football, art, and dance. Living in the midst of deprivation, these children have learnt to break social taboos and take control of their own lives, thanks to the efforts of their "bhaiya", Sylvester Peters, a motivational trainer by profession, who has organised these children under "Angels".

Sylvester started teaching a few children at his Vikaspuri home as a 13-year-old. Now at 34, his academy has expanded to include nearly 60 children. "These kids would have fallen into a life of drugs and crime if they were left without any aid. Now, they are dedicated to their studies and want to make something good out of their lives," he says.

"We wake up early for football practice everyday, and as a result, none of us miss school anymore," 14-year-old Pooja says. She has had to break through gender lines to play her favourite game. Her mother says teachers at the local MCD school were impressed by the change in her daughter. "Her English and science marks have improved, and she is so involved in the sport. Neighbours might say she is not behaving like a girl but I can see that she is doing well in life," Radha, Pooja's mother, says.

"Our studies have improved because we all help each other in class. We also teach each other skills like sewing, which we learn from our parents," 16-year-old Laddan says.

Visiting St Mark's is a high point for these children, who say they couldn't have imagined being inside the precincts of a private school. "It was very nice playing there. We were so nervous because we had never played with anyone outside. Now we will play again soon," 17-year-old Chandan Sharma says. 19-year-old Sanjay is going to sit for the Class X Board exams through open school. "I have worked in a private school but this time we were guests there," he says.

"It is our goal to make sure that our students are sensitised to the needs of others. When we learnt about Angels, I decided to help these children since it is a wonderful effort being made with no outside support," Anjali Aggarwal, principal of St Mark's School, Paschim Vihar, says.

The students of St Marks contributed money for 20 complete football kits for the children at Angels. They also donated books, stationery and clothes for the children from Angels.

Class XI student Kunal Malhotra was part of the team that played the friendly against the children from Angels. He says: "It was a huge learning experience for us, to visit the slums and interact with the children. Sylvester Peters told us all about Angels. I never knew that slum children could be so well spoken and confident."

Heading: Wife to Max: come clean on death - Indian Express
Content:
After Khosla ka Ghosla, Dibakar Banerjee hopes to hit the jackpot again with Oye Lucky Lucky Oye

Dibakar Banerjee does not like comparisons to Hrishikesh Mukherjee. "He had his style of filmmaking and I have mine," he defends, "the only point of similarity is that we both made films about ordinary people."

Banerjee's directorial debut, Khosla ka Ghosla about a middle-class family caught in a land scam, hit bull's-eye with the multiplex going audience. Expectations are now riding high on his next film, Oye Lucky Lucky Oye. But the pressure rests easy on Banerjee's shoulders even as he excitedly talks about his new film. "It's about a thief who's very special," he says, "unlike other thieves, who never want anyone to find out anything about them, this guy wants everyone to know he's the one who committed the crime. He has a talent for stealing and he's very proud of his 'craft'. If you haven't figured out it's him, he'll call you and tell you that he did it!"

It's obvious that Banerjee is attracted to stories that are a little out of the ordinary. And, he says, that tendency also affected the choice of his movie's leading man, Abhay Deol. "Abhay likes to look at the unusual side of things. He doesn't believe in doing what everyone else does. In that sense, we're very alike," he explains, "Moreover he's a very intense actor. That doesn't usually come out since he plays it cool, but he's one of the most focused actors I've met. This intensity of his will take him a long way," he predicts.

Banerjee is, in fact, very upbeat about all the actors in his movie. "We've deliberately not repeated any of the cast members from Khosla. We wanted to work with old and established actors like Paresh Rawal and also some new faces. In fact, there are 10 new actors in this film, five of whom have never acted before."

The music in his films, says Banerjee, also plays a very important role in the narration. "In most Indian movies, music plays a very important role in drawing the audience to the theatres and in providing breaks throughout the narration," he says, "I'm not entirely comfortable with that idea. So instead, even the songs are pushed into the background and become an integral part of the storytelling." The soundtrack of Khosla was a huge hit for the freshness of its sound and Banerjee has made sure that this time too, the audience has something new to listen to. "We've recruited a young talent called Sneha Khandwala. She actually went backpacking in Haryana and Punjab and brought back the old, forgotten melodies and poetry from those regions. You'll hear a lot of folk music on this soundtrack; we've even got folk singers singing here."

Heading: ‘I earn for two reasons: fighting polls, and fending for my kids’ - Indian Express
Content:
Top CII executive Jayant Bhuyan's wife says hospital still has a lot to do: 'deal with erring doctor'

After meeting with the top management of Max Healthcare, Ramola Bhuyan on Thursday asked the hospital authorities to come clean with the "sequence of events" that led to her husband Jayant K Bhuyan's death on October 6 following a bypass surgery.

Bhuyan was deputy director general of the Confederation of Indian Industry.

While both parties came out "satisfied" after the meeting, Ramola said a lot needs to be done before they reach an agreement. "The hospital officials spoke openly about what resulted in my husband's death," she told Newsline late Thursday evening, following the meeting. "But having said that, a lot needs to be done even now.

"Given that the error resulted in my husband's death, someone has to take responsibility. I trust the Max administration to deal with the erring doctor thereafter."

On their part, Max authorities hope the matter would not snowball into an extended legal affair. "We have explained the events that transpired that day and the family is well informed about the sequence of events. The way the meeting went, we can say that the patient's wife was satisfied with our explanation, which was based on a detailed investigation," said Pervez Ahmed, executive medical director, Max Healthcare.

Hospital authorities maintain that though unfortunate, the incident was not a result of medical negligence; they are calling it an "accident".

According to the Bhuyan family, they are yet to arrive at a decision whether to move the court against the hospital. "Going to court will be our last resort," Ramola said. "We are hoping that the matter is not dragged any further. All we want is that the culprit (doctor "responsible") should not get away and it should be for everyone to see.

"This should become an example and should bring in a change in the system as doctors get away with a lot and patients pay for their mistakes."

Bhuyan died after a triple bypass heart surgery at Max Devki Devi Heart and Vascular Institute. His wife has said that the hospital authorities had informed her, soon after Bhuyan's death, that the patient had died because of an "accident" during the surgery. The hospital authorities, she said, told her that a wrong tube was inserted into Bhuyan's heart, which released oxygen into his brain in a large dose, leading to brain damage.

Bhuyan, 58, was admitted to Max Hospital in Gurgaon after a heart attack on September 29. He was later moved to Max Devki Devi Institute at Saket. An angiography revealed that three of his arteries were blocked and that he needed an immediate open-heart surgery. Dr Inderjit Virdi led the team that operated on him.

Heading: Jammers on their way, Tihar turns no-cellular jail - Indian Express
Content:
The election fervour is here to stay. That's the first impression one gets after meeting Balram Bari at his tea stall in one of the narrowest lanes at Khari Baoli, in the Walled City. After all, he has been at it — fighting elections — for almost two decades now.

As the election campaigning gathers heat, Bari, who owns the small tea stall, sits comfortably in his own small world of politics, with sundry admirers in tow. Come November 29, and the 42-year-old 'seasoned politician' would fight his 11th polls. This year included, Bari has filed nominations 13 times.

And he has lost all of them.

"When I was young, an astrologer had told me that I would fight my first election at age 25 and, after years of struggle, would enjoy raj yog when I turn 43," Bari says, somewhat smugly. He turns 43 next year. "That means I win either this time (Assembly elections) or the Lok Sabha polls next year."

For the record, Bari has tried his luck in elections of every sort: from municipal to Assembly to the big one — the Lok Sabha polls.

Inside the narrow, pitch-dark Gandhi Lane, close to Fatehpuri Mosque, Bari has been running his tea stall for more than 20 years. Having dropped out of school after failing in Mathematics, Bari now supports his family (75-year-old mother, wife, and four children) with his humble monthly income of Rs 6,000. But there are no complaints.

Contesting an election costs money: merely filing a nomination for the Assembly polls costs a candidate Rs 5,000; and the amount is exactly the double if the election in question if for the Lok Sabha.

But a nonchalant Bari says, "I earn only for two reasons: first, to fight elections and, second, to feed my children."

His debut in the world of politics was in the 1989 Lok Sabha elections, when he pitched himself against Congress's J P Aggarwal, now the Delhi Congress chief. Bari had won 15 votes then. His last, the 2007 Municipal Corporation of Delhi elections, saw him fetching 115 votes.

Of the 13 time he filed nomination, it was rejected twice on varied grounds. But there's no sign of dejection even after stumbling on so many occasions: "I do not have to campaign; my voters come and seek me. I treat them to a cup of tea at my stall and listen to all their problems patiently."

Bari says during election time, he publishes pamphlets and goes and meets everyone in the area.

He might not win elections but for Gandhi Gali he has become a political commentator. "Delhi politics has changed dramatically in the last 20 years; there is no place for political workers now," he says. "Only those with money are given tickets these days."

The forecast this time? 1,500 votes, Bari says. "I got election I-cards made for nearly 1,500 people, of which nearly 700 were first-timers. I am hoping that all of them would vote for me." But the twinkle in his eyes returns soon: "Next year, I am surely going to win the Lok Sabha elections."

Heading: Honey, they shrunk the shrubs: Slowdown hits garden economy as well - Indian Express
Content:
Tihar Jail inmates would soon get no signal even if they manage to have mobile phones sneaked in, against the law. Reason: jail officials have begun the process of putting up jammers in an attempt to beef up security inside the prison.

The move comes just about a year after noted criminal Sharafat Sheikh was found with two cellphones, purportedly running his drug racket from the confines of his jail cell.

The idea, Tihar Jail officials said, is to tighten security at Asia's largest prison and stop use of cellphones within the prison. "The trial run for the jammers had been on for a few days. We will soon start the operation with installing equipment in four cells," Director General (Prisons) B K Gupta said.

Calling it a "preventive measure," he said the step would decrease the possibility of illegal use of mobile phones by inmates, either by possessing them or with the help of visitors. "We have always taken precautions to avert such incident and installation of jammers should be seen as a move to tighten security," he said. It is meant to halt the flow of prohibited objects inside the jail."

As a pilot project, three of the four jammers would be installed at Jail numbers one, three and four of Tihar. These jails primarily house terrorists and noted criminals. The fourth jammer would be put up at Rohini Jail.

"We are committed to presenting Tihar as a model jail for other prisons," Gupta said, "and jammers are being installed as part of the bigger exercise in which we had also installed as many as 259 CCTVs."

Sunil Gupta, Tihar's law officer, added, "This step was necessary, especially with frequent news from many states about inmates found with mobile phones. We do not want to land in any embarrassing situation."

Tihar Jail officials were left in a spot when Sharafat Sheikh, the alleged drug lord, was found possessing two mobile phones, which he purportedly used to run his racket from inside the cell. Delhi Police's narcotics department had intercepted calls made and received from Tihar in September last year. In searches that followed, two mobiles were found from Sheikh's cell.

The move to install jammers will have no impact on security officers as no one — not even officials — is allowed to carry mobile phones inside the prison. Officials use only landline phones.

Heading: Two under way, seven start in a year: Metro corridors put on fast tack - Indian Express
Content:
The vibrant, glossy streets of Gurgaon and the bustling industrial belt of Noida might get a tad smoggier as the natural purifiers that lined the premises of companies in the NCR towns go missing.

With the economic slowdown now a stark reality, most companies that once fenced their offices with potted plants and neatly trimmed shrubs — hired on rent from nearby nurseries — are packing off the plants to cut costs.

The Capital and the NCR is dotted with nurseries that offer potted plants on rent at a substantial fee, and follow it up with maintenance staff. But with the year-end targets yet to be met, corporate offices are cutting all possible overhead costs, and the leafy pots are not spared. "BPOs have started cutting down on the number of rented plants. Two of my clients from Gurgaon sent back half the plants that we had supplied last week," says Pragya Nair, who runs Plantex Nursery in Vasant Kunj and caters to 100-odd corporate clients.

Nair's nursery provides indoor and outdoor plants to corporate offices on monthly rentals — an average of Rs 50 and Rs 100. "One of our trained staff checks them every alternate day and circulates them," says Nair, apprehensive that the coming months may be worse. "A lot of export houses in NCR, which earlier showed off their offices with fancy orchids and ferns, have totally cut out on plants."

Most nurseries set a minimum limit to the number of plants that go for each rental and follow it up with a one-year contract. This clause, says Manoj of Plants World in Adhchini, has helped him secure his clients for now but is apprehensive of the future once the contract ends. The only plants surviving the shrinking pockets, it seems, are money plants and lucky bamboo.

"Last month we had retrieved a money plant from the cabin of a finance officer since it had withered," Nair says, "but the officer requested us to put it back within a day. It hardly has a few green leaves on it."

Among other plants popular with indoor office spaces are the Dracaena, which consumes a lot of rubber and ink toxic, Syngoniums, and Palms. "Most of my office clients prefer lucky bamboo and money plants these days," says Dev Gujral of Garden Hut at Adhchini.

But landscaping gardens, Gujral says, is no longer a greener option for plants nurseries like his. "For an upcoming mall in Manesar, we were supposed to lay out a garden with orchids and shrubs. Now, they just want us to carpet the area with grass."

With most housing projects across the NCR either stalling their projects or finishing them in a jiffy, Gujral says gardens are hardly on their list of priorities. "There was a garden landscaping that we were supposed to do for a housing society in Ghaziabad but the company has put that on hold."

In winters, most plant nurseries changed the plants with lilies, anthurium and orchids but nursery owners are not sure if the companies will buy this seasonal change as flowers cost more than their leafy counterparts.

Reema Khatri, who runs Natural Flowers in Jangpura, sites a similar experience: "Landscaping costs have surely been cut down. We were supposed to do a garden for a mall in Noida but their officials have now slashed our budget by 50 per cent."

At an average of Rs 75 and Rs 95, Khatri provides plants to malls, banks and BPOs. "Some of my clients have inquired for revised rates if they reduce the number of plants and cut down on our maintenance services," she says.

For Ravi Vats, who runs Green Environment in Noida, the beginning of this week did not bring in good news either. "One of my big clients, a BPO in Gurgaon, sent back more than 70 per cent of the plants we had supplied.

Heading: Chatted on the Net, fell into police net - Indian Express
Content:
With the city's first two Metro rail corridors now under execution, the project's nodal agency is now planning to expedite the progress of the remaining seven corridors that together comprise the Mumbai Metro Rail masterplan with an ambitious target: to start work on these corridors in a year's time.

A senior Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) official said that a plan is being worked out to speed up the process of taking up corridors for implementation. "We want to start work on the remaining corridors within the next one year. It's not possible to start all of them in one go, but a plan to initiate the work on the seven corridors has been presented before Chief Minister Vilasrao Deshmukh," the official said.

A senior bureaucrat added that it is now essential to expedite the work on the Metro corridors rather than going phase wise as proposed earlier, under which the routes would all be operational only in 2021. "There is acute need for more transportation options in the city and going phase-wise would further burden the existing network by 2021," the bureaucrat reasoned.

Interestingly, the MMRDA has made up its mind to opt for the public-private partnership model for the remaining corridors except for the "most challenging" Corridor III -Colaba-Bandra, which involves a high viability gap fund. The bureaucrat said that financial models would be cleared by the state government for each corridor separately, but at present PPP is the best option available for the MMRDA. This comes following a series of flip-flops on the funding model for the second route - after constituting the Mumbai Metro Rail Corporation on the lines of the government-funded projects of the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation, the state decided to revert to the PPP model for the Charkop-Bandra-Mankhurd corridor.

"As far as possible, PPP model would be adopted for remaining Metro routes expect Colaba-Bandra as the VGF is Rs 9,000 crore. For the third route we're considering various options, but still there is no final decision on it," the bureaucrat added.

According to the bureaucrat, the only hindrance with the PPP model is the VGF. "We can pose the VGF to Government of India like in case of the Charkop-Bandra-Mankhurd metro corridor. The other option is to raise it through sale of real estate," he said.

The MMRDA also plans to utilise the space in the metro stations for commercial use to make the Metro corridors more financially viable. "This option is one of the key resource generators for MMRDA which will take care of the remaining corridors. With the commercial exploitation, we expect to bring down the VGF by nearly half the amount," he said.

* Versova-Andheri-Ghatkopar (11.2 km)
* Charkop-Bandra-Mankhurd (32 km)
* Colaba Bandra (19.85 km)

PHASE-II (2011-2016)

Heading: House collapse: Family added an illegal floor - Indian Express
Content:
BANK FRAUD: How cops nabbed woman in Rs 2-crore transfer

It was through a chat friend that the Cuffe Parade police managed to net Kapol Bank employee Malathi Kanchan who transferred Rs 2 crore from the bank's funds into bogus accounts in Kolkata and Punjab.

According to the police, Abdul Wahid, Kanchan's former bank colleague — who had been arrested last week—- had revealed that Kanchan frequently chatted with an online friend from Ajmer and was very close to him. The police established contact with the friend and set a trap, eventually arresting Kanchan on Wednesday.

"Kanchan transferred the money via Real Transaction Gross System on October 24 and after she learnt that the bank was planning to file police complaint about the transaction, she stopped coming to work from October 31. On November 6, we arrested Wahid after learning that he had been sacked by the bank two years ago. During interrogation, Wahid described how the heist had been planned and revealed the names of Kanchan and her beau Shashikumar Shetty. He told us that Kanchan frequently chatted with one Kapil from Ajmer, whom she had met online some months back and considered him a brother," said assistant police inspector Tukaram Mane, who is investigating the case.

Mulling over a plan to arrest Kanchan, the police realised that Kapil could be their best bet. "Wahid had worked with Kanchan in the same IT department and was aware of her platonic relationship with Kapil. He also knew Kapil's e-mail ID. On our instructions, Wahid spoke to Kapil pretending to be in some kind of trouble. He expressed a desire to meet Kanchan in this regard and requested Kapil to persuade Kanchan for a meeting. Obliging Kapil, Kanchan reached Nariman Point expecting to meet Wahid, but found police waiting for her instead," said Mane.

Incidentally, Wahid had also been arrested in a similar fashion. The cops had told the Kapol bank's officials to call him to the office citing a pending clearance of his dues. He walked into the bank and was arrested.

The cops said Kapil played a major role in Kanchan's arrest. At the same time they stressed that he was merely a friend of the accused and did not have any role to play in the crime as he was not aware of it. Now, they are trying to trace Shetty who they claim is the mastermind behind the heist. "The accused opened two accounts in UTI-Axis Bank in Kolkata. The money from one of the accounts was transferred to three other accounts. A sum of Rs 24 lakh was transferred to the account of one Balwinder Singh from Jalandhar. A team will go to Punjab to track it," said Mane.

According to the police, all the three accused are IT professionals and very well know how the bank functions. While Kanchan and Wahid knew about Kapol bank's system, they suspect that Shetty may have been reportedly a former UTI-Axis Bank employee.

Heading: Finest in Indian photojournalism to be honoured today - Indian Express
Content:
Civic and housing authorities both knew, neither took action

An extra floor, built illegally, might have caused the collapse in Sayyed House that left six dead on Wednesday. A family had built the floor in 1991 and officials suspect the extra load might have been too much for the 71-year-old structure to bear.

A report submitted to MHADA mention various causes: old age, wear and tear, additions and alterations such as the illegal floor, kitchen and toilet at the rear, besides piling and construction adjacent to the building.

The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) and housing authority MHADA were both aware of the illegal floor but neither took any action over the last 17 years.

"The structure originally had the ground floor plus four storeys. The fifth floor was built in 1991; a sixth floor terrace was developed subsequently," said an official from the BMC's building proposal department (city), who wished not to be named.

In 1992, the family had carried out repairs funded by the MHADA repair board. The housing authority was informed about the illegal construction then, BMC officials said. "In our remarks on the building it was mentioned that the building had a non-tallying portion (illegal construction). MHADA knew about it," he added.

While the BMC and the MHADA are authorised to take action for such illegal constructions in a cessed building, both authorities turned a blind eye. "We never got any reply from MHADA to take action on the illegal floor," the civic official said.

Officials said that the Sayyed family also planned to build rooms on the sixth floor last year. That plan was, however, dropped.

MHADA deputy chief engineer Balbir Sehgal said that after the BMC had pointed out the illegal construction, the civic administration was directed to take action. "We don't know why no action was taken," he said.

The owners of the building, however, refused to accept that the fifth floor was "unauthorised". "As per the original plan when the building was made in 1936, it had the ground plus five floors. However, we did not completely utilise the fifth floor and only part of it was built and used for housing purposes. The rest was used like a terrace. When repairs were carried in 1992, we completely built the fifth floor," said Dr Farzaan Sayyed.

Sehgal said many factors led to the collapse, including old age and the piling work. "Many parts of the building like wooden panels were decomposing and the structure could not bear the load," he said.

MHADA had proposed repair work in August but the owners allegedly refused to cooperate, saying they were in a dispute and in talks with the developer. It takes at least three or four months for permission and clearance before actual repair can start.

The building is currently being demolished and the rescued residents will be shifted.

The India Press Photo Awards 2008 — instituted by the Ramnath Goenka Foundation in 2004— will be given away at a glitzy ceremony at Express Towers, Nariman Point, in Mumbai on Friday.

Actor Salman Khan will be the chief guest at the function. Actor-director Anupam Kher, who is the guest of honour, and director-producer Subhash Ghai, special guest, will unveil photographs from the Express archives.

The awards are an attempt to identify, promote and reward excellence in photojournalism and documentary photography. "We, at the Express group, believe visuals often tell stories better than words and try to celebrate photographs on our pages. We are proud to be part of an effort that showcases the best of photojournalism in India because the awards not just honour the best talent in the industry but underscore the importance of visuals in print journalism as well," says Shekhar Gupta, editor-in-chief of The Indian Express.

The response to IPPA 200— sponsored by Canon — has been overwhelming: 8,801 entries from 226 photographers. The panel of judges — renowned photojournalists Prashant Panjiar, Pablo Bartholomew and Harsh Man Rai — will choose one grand prize-winning image and one winner from each of the 18 categories. Alok Bhardawaj, senior vice-president, Canon India Pvt Ltd, will deliver the closing speech.

The Ramnath Goenka Picture of the Year will go to the photographer whose picture demonstrates an outstanding level of visual creativity and journalistic skill. The winner gets a cash prize of Rs 1.5 lakh. The award-winning photographs will be displayed at an exhibition in Mumbai, which will travel throughout the country.

The award categories are: Arts & Entertainment (Single and Story), Contemporary Issues (Single and Story), Nature & Environment (Single and Story), Portrait (Single and Story), Sports Action (Single and Story), People in News (Single and Story), Daily Life (Single and Story), General News Story, Spot News (Single and Story) and the Winning Photograph.

Heading: Religious books, meditation keep Sadhvi busy in jail  - Indian Express
Content:
At home Sunil Pant is an articulate and successful Member of Parliament who fights for the rights of people of his country, Nepal, whether they are homosexual or heterosexual. On a visit to Mumbai, the only openly gay MP from the Himalayan country marched with lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and inter-sex (LGBTI) people in Azad Maidan to campaign against the alleged violence perpetrated by the police against sexual minorities in Bangalore and other parts of India.

On Thursday, the city's LGBTI community gathered and raised slogans such as, 'Save Democracy, Protect Sexual Minorities' and 'Dushmani Hatao, Dostana Badhao' (Remove enmity, encourage friendship).

"We have moved from being a marginalised and persecuted lot who were thrown out of homes, schools and jobs to people who have human rights and are now protected by the police, the same people who once harassed us," said Pant. Pant is the founder of the Blue Diamond Society (2003), a network of 20 groups and organisations working on HIV/AIDS, human rights and social justice issues for sexual and gender minorities in Nepal.  "India is the world's biggest democracy. It's shocking and saddening to see that basic human rights of sexual and gender minorities are denied," said the 34-year-old former software engineer. Pant has just returned from Bangalore after meeting with Sangama members and the transgenders who were allegedly subjected to police brutality, illegal detention, custodial torture and sexual assault.

"In Nepal, the LGBTI communities were part of the campaign for garnering votes for the Communist Party of Nepal (UML)," said Pant. "They approached me to campaign and I managed to secure 15,500 votes. It makes a statement that LGBTI people are interested in matters of politics and governance and not just sex," he said.

"The campaign not only gave LGBTI issues visibility but a platform to negotiate for rights. The Nepal government now recognises the third gender (LBGTIs)," he added. Pant is also working with the government to sanction a shelter for homeless LBGTI population and poverty alleviation of sexual minorities. "It is one thing to clean up the city and stop transgenders from begging but one must provide them with alternative means of living," said Pant. He says that in Nepal, transgenders are now trained as beauticians and hair dressers while lesbians run a public transport system.

"India is a very big country and a single strategy may not work," said Pant. "However, I'm sure it won't be long before a political party will tap the LGBTI vote bank¯there are millions of untapped votes."

Heading: Twist of fate: Collapse hastens family shift - Indian Express
Content:
Sadhvi Pragya Singh Thakur who is presently lodged at the Byculla jail is keeping herself busy by reading the Ramcharita Manas and Ramayan available in the jail library. The sadhvi who will soon be shifted from the jail does not interact with anyone and is closely guarded by jail officials.

 Pragya was arrested in connection with the September 29, Malegaon blasts and was in the custody of Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS). On November 3, she was sent to judicial custody but was brought to Mumbai as the ATS wanted to conduct a narco-analysis test on her. She has been at the Byculla prison since then.

Jail sources said Pragya is kept in a separate cell with no other inmate and two officials guard her cell round the clock. The police don't want to take any chance with her security, as there is a risk to her life from other inmates. The Byculla jail houses inmates like Fahmida Hanif, involved in the Gateway of India and Zaveri bazaar bomb blast case. Fahmida who has a record of picking up fights inside the jail is alleged to have bashed up Zaheera Shaikh the key witness turned accused in the Best Bakery case, when she was in the prison.

Jail Superintendent Sudhir Kingre confirmed that Pragya was being kept in a separate cell. "Yes she is been kept in a separate cell because of security concerns and also because she is not originally an accused of our jail. She will soon be shifted, till then all necessary care is been taken," Kingre said.

Sources said Pragya is an early riser and wakes up at 5 am. This time is utilised by her to meditate as there is silence till others wake up. She does various yoga asanas before having her bath and breakfast. The breakfast in jail comprises of one bowl of poha or upma, one glass of milk and tea and one banana.

After the breakfast, she heads back to the cell where she reads the religious scripts like Ramayan and Ramcharita Manas for hours, till lunch is served at 12 noon. Sources said she also has some books on improving meditation and yoga skills.

Talking about the Sadhiv's stay in the prison Kingre said, "She attends the daily prayer held in the open ground inside the jail, at 8 am, after which she spends her time alone inside the cell. This is what I have heard from my staff." He added that they are are giving her food as per state directives, which includes one bowl of rice, daal, one leafy vegetable and three chapatis for lunch and dinner. After lunch she stays in the cell, resting and reading.  

Sadhvi's lawyer Navin Chomal who meets her on Saturday and Tuesday inside the prison, said that she doesn't speak much. He added that during their meeting she discusses only about the case and no personal things. He further said that after the scientific test conducted on her during police custody, she was not keeping well but inside the jail her health is improving.

Heading: Before state could clear the first, another encroachment on varsity land - Indian Express
Content:
Three-year-old Sayyed Rehan cries tugging at his mother's salwar. "Amma, I want to go back home and sleep on my bed," is what he tells his amma often. Little does he know that his home is no longer there. A day after Sayyed House in Nagdevi Street at Crawford market collapsed killing six members of the Sayyed family, hope is the prevailing sentiment among the family members.

"Just two days ago we decided that we will move out of the house and now in a twist of fate we are actually moving. This episode has taught us that a few seconds can change your whole life," said Sayyed Rumana Fauzaan, sister-in-law of Dr Sayyed Imran who died in Wednesday's accident.

The distant family members have come from all over the country to give support. The family is now staying at the nearby Jannat house. They will remain there till the last rites are over. Within two days, the family will be moving to MHADA-provided transit camp at Colaba. "We have been moving from house to house. It has been a tedious time. Neighbours have shown tremendous support by providing us with a temporary roof," says another relative, Umera Sayyed.

Refuting allegations of illegal construction by their late brother, the family is puzzled at the civic body's apathy. "No BMC official ever visited the place; we have all the legal documents which can prove that the fifth floor is legal. Even if it was illegal then why did the civic body not take any action against us? They could have done that but only after this accident did they choose to speak," says Rumana Fauzaan.

Seeing the tragedy on television, a close family friend, Zahur Ahmed, who was in Bangalore, reached there immediately. "When I saw images of my friend's dead body, I was in a state of shock. Dr Imran Sayyed was like a brother to me. It has not yet sunk in that his two children, Omer and Mariam, will no longer say salaam to me," says Ahmed. He has been living near the Sayyed family house for the past 20 years. "Why did the kids have to die such a tragic death? Who should be blamed?" he asks.

At the Sayyed house, Fauzia Khader Sayyed, mother of Dr Imran Sayyed and a strong matriarchal figure is yet to realise that her eldest son is no more. "Where is my son, Imran? Bring him back," she wails. Dr Sayyed and his wife Dr Rihana Sayyed were both visiting doctors at Bacha's Memorial Bellevue Nursing home. Dr Rihana also took tuition classes. "Rihana's students' exams were approaching. Hence she did not want to leave the place. They had decided that after this exam season, they will move to a different location," said Rumana.

The police are investigating the matter. "We have written letters to the BMC and MHADA. We have asked them to file a report as soon as they find the cause of the accident. Only then can we say who was responsible," said senior inspector Samsher Pathan.

Political Twist
The collapse of Sayyed house has taken a political twist with the Samajwadi Party demanding that the police book a case against the developer and architect of the structure next to Sayyed House, who dug the pit that is said to have caused the collapse. Pydhonie police, however, seem adamant in investigating in their own capacity. "Who are the Samajwadi party to demand anything?" said Samsher Khan Pathan, Senior Police Inspector of Pydhoni police station. "Let me make it clear, we are conducting a technical and professional investigation. After we finish our enquiries with the BMC, MHADA and take the statements of the owners will we name any accused. Some people are trying to blackmail the developers," he added.

Heading: Autonomous signals for traffic control - Indian Express
Content:
Mumbai University says builder was clearing way for housing societies as police looked on;HC had ordered state earlier to clear another encroachment by December

With just less than two months left for the Bombay High Court deadline asking the state government to clear encroachments on its land in Kalina, near Bandra Kurla Complex, the University of Mumbai has complained of yet another instance of encroachment.

According to the University, their land located near Grand Hyatt hotel was allegedly 'cleared' by workers belonging to a builder to pave way for some housing societies last Thursday. Fearing trouble, University security officers later approached the Vakola police.

"Last Friday, the police arrived at the spot while the workers were carrying on with their work. But instead of stopping the workers of the builder, they threatened us and asked us to let them carry on their work. They even asked us to show the land documents. When we asked them to come to our office as the papers were kept there, they refused. Then we decided to inform higher authorities of the University," said a security officer on condition of anonymity.

The officer said the workers belonged to Mishra Builders.

Late Wednesday night, the University filed an FIR against Mishra Builders and the policemen who were present on the disputed land site last Friday.

Meanwhile, senior police inspector S Nekalikar of Vakola Police station said, "The University officials did not show us any documents. How can we ascertain if that land belongs to them? We acted appropriately¿ we have nothing against the University."

Pro vice-chancellor A D Sawant said, "We have received a report from the security department and our investigations are on." Sawant added, "The matter is subjudice. The university is taking the necessary steps to ensure that the encroachments are cleared within deadline."

In May last year, Justice J N Patil and Justice S C Dharmadhikari had directed the state government to clear encroachment of over 600 shanties on a land in Kalina belonging to the University and 'hand over the University land, back to it, for its developmental activities' by April 30, 2007. The deadline was later extended till December 31, 2007. The principal secretary of the housing department then stated that it was too early to carry out survey of over 600 hutments, issue notices to them and analyse their documents till the deadline, after which the high court extended the deadline by a year. The University vice-chancellor, Dr Vijay Khole, in a letter dated February 12, 2008 to the lawyer representing it, Rui Rodrigues, stated the encroachment on the Kalina land is not only increasing but illegal sale of structures constructed on the land had also started.
