Heading: Neighbourliness - Indian Express
Content:
Assembly elections start today. In the first phase, 39 out of the state's 90 constituencies will go to the polls. In the phases to follow, much action is expected; 1089 candidates will vie for 70 seats in Delhi; the Congress has fielded candidates from the youth wing of the party in 35 seats; 862 election meetings have already been held in Jammu and Kashmir. And, as always, there is much speculation about what the electioneering, and possible results, mean for the Big Event planned for a few months down the line, the general elections. And while such speculation is always entertaining, the sad truth is it won't be very useful.

There are several reasons why. The first is that many of the states going to the polls have particularly strong histories of anti-incumbency, which may not be replicated across the rest of the country to the same degree. They may buck this trend; but even if they do, it would be difficult to mean that pro- or anti-incumbency swings observed in these could be considered to have any validity in other states.

More to the point, it is far from certain whether any of this matters in terms of which overarching coalition will take power after the next general elections. The last polls were won by the UPA following shrewd alliance-making; the DMK trounced Jayalalithaa in Tamil Nadu, for example, and in Bihar the Congress-Paswan-Left-Lalu alliance crushed the NDA. India is the sum of its states; the states will vote for different reasons — perhaps state performance, perhaps national leadership, perhaps a combination of the two that's unique to this election — and then what will matter is the arithmetic of alliances. So what should we really be thinking about when we look at these elections, which feature in most parts a straight battle between the Congress and the BJP? Rather than focusing on minutiae of local swings for or against one or another of the two major parties, we should perhaps look at how the two parties are balancing interests within themselves. Are they able to control rebellious factions, for example, the sort of people who will object when tickets have to be handed out in large numbers to demanding allies? It's good that we're already keeping one eye open in that direction.

Heading: Semi-automatic - Indian Express
Content:
Raj Thackeray's goons may have made the most noise, but crass regionalism has raised its ugly head of late in many parts of the country. In Bihar, in retaliation to the MNS campaign, mobs have gone on a rampage and a Maharashtra IAS officer was attacked. Nitish Kumar's five JD(U) MPs resigned from the Lok Sabha. In Tamil Nadu, the DMK's Karunanidhi wants to project that it outdoes rival Dravidian parties in protecting Sri Lankan Tamils, even if it means twisting the arm of the central government. In Andhra Pradesh, Chandrababu Naidu, who had resolutely opposed the formation of Telangana, has now changed his stance, fearing that otherwise he would have to pay the price at the next assembly polls. In Rajasthan, Chief Minister Vasundhara Scindia has launched her poll campaign playing up regional sentiment and adopting a confrontationist stance towards the Centre, on the lines of Narendra Modi's campaign asserting Gujarati pride. In Assam the spate of recent terrorist attacks is largely attributable to the schism between the original settlers and migrants.

Already ripple effects of the dangerous game played by Thackeray are being felt elsewhere. In Haryana a gang of lumpens issued an ultimatum to 15,000 Maharashtrian families, their neighbours: leave or else. In Chandigarh some vague north Indian organisation hopes to garner TV attention by threatening to throw out Maharashtrians.

Can a citizen of India really be termed an outsider in his own country? It is in any case debatable how one decides who is an outsider and who a son of the soil. The MNS claims it wants to protect the character of Mumbai which is being destroyed by migrants from north India. The supporters of the MNS and Sena, mostly Marathas, believe that they should reap the benefits that accrue from living in the country's commercial capital. But the Kolis, the fishing community that was the original dwellers of the island of Mumbai, can in turn dub the Marathas, who hail from the plains of Marathwada and not the coastal belt, outsiders. The Kolis did not benefit financially from the transformation of their once sleeping fishing villages into a major port and a commercial hub. And, of course, neither the Kolis nor the Marathas played much part in setting up the city's financial institutions, its major landmarks, the film industry, philanthropic bodies, cultural movements, hospitals and educational institutions. It was the British, Parsees, Gujaratis, along with entrepreneurs, artistes and innovators from all over India who made Mumbai what it is today. In fact at the time of the division of Bombay state into Gujarat and Maharashtra in 1960, Gujarat maintained it had equal claim to Bombay since the city had almost similar numbers of Gujaratis and Maharashtrians then.

As with Mumbai, the demographics of many other Indian cities has radically altered. In Delhi, for instance, the original inhabitants of the walled city were swamped by the flood of Punjabi refugees who arrived after Partition. And in the last three decades, the city's demography has altered yet again. Similarly, the original Haryanvi farmers of Gurgaon have long been outnumbered by lakhs of new apartment dwellers, who see themselves as living in a suburb of Delhi.

A country's prosperity and progress depends on the synergy of its people. If people are to be confined to the regions where they were born, the very idea of nationhood is lost. It is troubling when irresponsible regional parties whip up chauvinist sentiment and promote an agenda of divisiveness. But it is far more disturbing when the government and the mainstream national parties refuse to take them on. In Maharashtra there is a strange silence from the main leaders in the state. The BJP, which prides itself on its nationalist outlook, does not want to upset its ally, the Shiv Sena. The Congress and NCP have been tacitly encouraging Raj Thackeray in the hope that he will cut into the support base of their main political rival, the Shiv Sena. The state chief minister sends a curious signal at this juncture by demanding that railway entrance examinations be conducted in Marathi. The mainstream parties forget that when one chooses to ride a tiger one runs the risk of being devoured, as was the case in Punjab where the Congress initially promoted the little known Bhindranwale for its own ends. If the regional parties are increasing in clout throughout India it is because of the vacuum created with the rapidly declining status of the national parties.

coomi.kapoor@expressindia.com

Heading: The genesis of Marc Chagall - Indian Express
Content:
Mahendra Singh Dhoni is a cricketer of striking grace on the field. Team sports are liable to be stricken by tremendous clashes of ego, but he has till now not betrayed any such frailty. In fact, his gesture of requesting Sourav Ganguly to conduct proceedings in his last overs in Test cricket at Nagpur showed as much. So, now with the Test captaincy too likely to be his for a long time, these are good tidings for the game. Cricket, pessimists fear, is in for a struggle to keep its practitioners interested in the older spirit that guided Test cricket. Dhoni has, of course, found success in all versions of the game, most spectacularly in its shortest version, Twenty20, for India in the world championships and for his Chennai squad in the IPL. But he is naturally possessed of a temperament that recalls the large-heartedness of earlier generations of cricketers.

Odd then that he is caught, off the field, in a controversy that is making his supporters petty and partisan. As reported in this newspaper, Dhoni had applied for a licence for a 9 mm pistol. This is categorised as a "prohibited weapon", and therefore requires more stringent clearance than most other firearms. The divisional commissioner of Chhotanagpur accordingly forwarded Dhoni's request for further clearance. His many fans evidently see this as a slight. There have been demonstrations against the official in Jamshedpur, Bokaro, Ranchi and Dhanbad. Some even want her sacked.

Why Dhoni wants such a weapon is for him to know. He is of course known to find relaxation in hitting the fast road on his motorbike. But given the absurd spectacle that has swept Jharkhand, he must ask himself if the 9 mm pistol is worth it. A cricketer is, after all, also known by the grace he shows off the field.

Heading: Owing the world - Indian Express
Content:
Asked the difference between art and eroticism, Picasso replied, "But there is no difference." Painters in the early 20th century had begun to express their inner lives on canvas as never before, plundering their sexual and psychological experiences for raw material. Wives and lovers became at once icons, muses, collaborators and victims. Of no artist was this more true than Marc Chagall, the great painter of love who changed his style every time he changed his woman. In art he invented a new language of rich colour, distorted forms and poetic metaphors that recorded the thrill and terror of the 20th century. In the relationships fuelling that work he often wreaked devastation. Born in 1887, Chagall endured war and revolution in St Petersburg and Moscow, exile in Paris, Berlin and New York, and Nazi terror in Marseilles, yet survived to enjoy a long, productive old age on the Côte d'Azur. All his life he painted the domes of his birthplace, Vitebsk, in Belarus, which were, for him, powerful symbols of his mother's love. "If I have made pictures, it is because I remember my mother, her breasts so warmly nourishing and exalting me, and I feel I could swing from the moon," Chagall said at 79. His young, illiterate, adoring mother, to whom Chagall was extremely close until her death in 1915, gave him robustness and optimism, but also a vulnerability in the form of his extreme dependence on women.

Aside from his mother, the first woman to have an impact on Chagall's work was Thea Brachmann. As a lonely impoverished student in St Petersburg in 1907 and 1908, Chagall painted in dingy 'potato' colours until he met 19-year-old Brachmann, a doctor's daughter also from Vitebsk. She posed nude for him — the first woman Chagall saw naked — and his palette suddenly began to blaze crimson, pink and rose, in paintings such as Red Nude. Broad-shouldered, big-boned, husky-voiced, energetic but liable to fits of gloom, Brachmann was a prototype of the woman Chagall chose. As well as being strong-minded and emotionally powerful, she was socially poised — Chagall's instinct as social climber never deserted him in love.

From an article by Jackie Wullschlager in 'The Daily Telegraph'

Heading: The day Nehru resigned - Indian Express
Content:
I was surprised to learn about the United Nation's worsening financial situation during my recent visit to the UN General Assembly as member of the Indian delegation. It is struggling to receive obligatory contributions by several countries, including the global economic superpowers. The total amount of unpaid contributions in just the UN's regular budget reached US$756 million and amounted to 40 per cent of total contributions in October 2008. For peacekeeping operations, the outstanding amount is a whopping US$2.9 billion. Remarkably, the biggest share of these defaults is borne by none other than the United States of America. The ongoing delay in receiving dues has begun to hurt UN's activities including its peacekeeping missions, as the secretariat is no longer able to make payments to contributors of troops and equipment.

I am equally surprised at India's parsimony. On one hand we are keen to assert our new status as an emerging superpower, on the other our contribution to the UN's regular budget matches those of Third World countries. India contributes a mere US$9.5 million per year to the regular budget.

What surprises me even more is that we contribute a massive US$80 million per year for a large number of welfare schemes run by the UN. If we were to divert even half of this amount to the UN's regular budget, the world would immediately start giving us our due respect. In any case, India's participation in peacekeeping operations in many parts of the world and our huge population living in poverty together ensure that our country is ultimately a net beneficiary of UN's budget. We receive some US$200 million a year from the UN under the World Food Program and for our participation in peacekeeping missions alone. In view of the financial and political interests at stake, I wonder why India has not voluntarily raised its obligatory contribution and at least matched China or Japan.

Embroiled in embargo

For the last 17 years, the UN General Assembly has deliberated over the 46-year-old economic sanctions imposed on Cuba. The premier body has repeatedly called upon all its member states to pay heed to the UN charter and international law, while rejecting laws or regulations with 'extra-territorial impact'. In simple terms, it has voiced its dissent over the coercive measures that impinge on the sovereignty of the South American nation. As it turns out, UN General Assembly's calls remain unheeded, its resolutions remain unimplemented, and Cuba continues to suffer under the embargo.

During my UN stint, I was able to unravel these effects of the Cuban embargo. The US has passed certain domestic laws which have enhanced the extra-territorial impact of the embargo. As a result, the Cuban economy has been hit badly. There has been considerable deterioration in the standard of living. Healthcare is particularly affected due to access controls on critical medical equipment and medicines. UN officials in Havana have noted that the embargo has had a negative impact on the society, economy and environment in Cuba. Further, it has restricted movement of UN's own staff and thus severely affected UN's programs in Cuba.

India has always respected the sovereignty of every nation and strongly opposed unilateral measures by any country that encroach upon the sovereignty of another, including attempts to extend the applications of its domestic laws extra-territorially to another sovereign state. During the recent general assembly session, I reiterated India's stand and vehemently denounced the unilateral encroachment of Cuba's sovereignty. Fortunately, it appears that calls to lift the sanctions have started coming from within the US. The US is a principal beneficiary of imports from Cuba and US businesses see substantial trade and investment opportunities in Cuba. Efforts by the US business community for access to the Cuban market have started yielding productive results.

Thank you for not smoking

The anti-smoking campaign of India's health minister has made its presence felt even at the UN. After many years of persistent effort, it recently passed a resolution banning smoking in its premises. Russia alone opposed the ban tooth and nail, while several other countries, including India, supported it. It is currently operational only in the New York headquarters, while other offices are exempt. When I spoke to Russia's permanent representative, he told me that he had no option, since Russia's foreign minister is a chain smoker.

The writer is a Congress MP in Rajya Sabha

Heading: State not serious on slum issue: BJP - Indian Express
Content:
Prosecutors in an Italian court Thursday asked the key middleman in the IAF's VVIP chopper deal whether the initials 'AP' in an alleged "budget sheet" for bribes to politicians referred to Ahmed Patel, the political secretary of UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi.

The middleman, Guido Haschke, who has consistently denied bribing Indian officials or politicians, replied that he did not know who or what 'AP' stood for.

As first reported by The Indian Express, Italian prosecutors had last month produced a handwritten document they alleged was a "budget" drawn up by two middlemen — Haschke and Christian Michel — which purportedly lists initials of Indian politicians and designations of bureaucrats and IAF officers who allegedly had to be "handled" to fix the Rs 3,546 crore deal.

The alleged "budget sheet" detailed how kickbacks of 51 million euros would be divided and under the heading "POL" — Haschke has claimed this referred to Indian politicians — there is a reference to "AP" against which "3 million euro" has been listed.

Another amount of 15/16 million euros was listed against "FAM" which is said to be "Family". Haschke has claimed the note was dictated to him by British consultant Michel during one of their meetings in 2008.

On Thursday, Italian prosecutor Eugenio Fusco asked Haschke during a court hearing in Busto Arsizio near Milan whether "AP" in the note was a reference to Ahmed Patel.

In his reply, the middlemen said he did not know what AP meant when he wrote it down. Haschke also denied any bribes were paid for the contract and said that the "budget sheet" was just an imaginary note drawn up and was never acted upon.

He also said the budget sheet was merely bragging by Michel about his Indian contacts and that Haschke tried to disassociate himself from the Briton.

Strongly denying any wrongdoing in the deal, Haschke also claimed to Indian interrogators in the court that no bribes were paid for the contract and that the money he received from AgustaWestland - in excess of 24 million euros - is justified as fees for engineering consultations.

Italian prosecutors also produced another note in court Thursday - a March 2008 fax by Michel to Peter Hulett, said to be the then head of region, govt sales at AgustaWestland's India office. The fax said that among the politicians who would use the choppers once acquired by India would be UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi and her senior advisors, including Ahmed Patel.

However, Sonia is not entitled to use government helicopters. She can use VIP aircraft only when she flies with the PM, President or ministers who are officially entitled to the aircraft. This fax by the British middleman has also been shared by the Italian side with the CBI team that is in Busto Arsizio for the hearing.

Michel has been elusive and no investigative agency has been able to reach him.

Haschke, who is facing a case in Italy for being part of a conspiracy to bribe Indian officials to ensure the AW 101 chopper was picked by the IAF, faced several questions from the Indian side and denied any irregularity.

But the Indian side did not ask Haschke to explain what AP, FAM or any of the other acronyms in the note - "DS", "JS AIR", "AFA", "DG Acquisition", CVC" etc - referred to, source said.

The middleman, who was quizzed about his association with former Air Chief S P Tyagi - named as an accused in the CBI case in the deal - denied that any money had been paid to the retired Indian officer. Haschke, sources said, admitted that he was in regular touch with three cousins of Tyagi who have also been named in the case.

In response to a question from the Indian side, Haschke said he was not aware if any money was paid to S P Tyagi.

The UPA government had come under pressure in connection with the alleged kickbacks last month after The Indian Express report on the budget sheet of the middlemen. The opposition BJP had demanded the government reveal what or who "AP" and "FAM" stand for. The party also said that it wants a detailed discussion in Parliament on "alleged payments to persons close to the ruling establishment" in connection with the controversial chopper deal and has accused the government of "running away from discussions".

The discussion did not take place as the Parliament session was abruptly called off midway.

Heading: Young mother found dead cradling live baby - Indian Express
Content:
Govt misguiding people on slum regularisation, says BJP city chief

Accusing the Vilasrao Deshmukh government of misguiding people on the issue of regularising slums that have come up in the city in 2000 or earlier — a promise made in the Congress-NCP manifesto during the 2004 elections — BJP Mumbai chief Gopal Shetty on Friday demanded that the government keep its word.

On the latest announcement by the government that slums erected till 2000 will be regularised, he feels the government is not serious on the issue.

Giving reasons for his suspicions, he said that during the 2004 polls, the government had declared 2000 as the cut-off year, but later said it was a printing error. "Now, with an eye on the 2009 elections, the government has announced that slums upto 2000 will be regularised, but a GR (government resolution) issued by the government imposes a condition that only those residing in Mumbai prior to 1995 would be the beneficiaries...this amounts to cheating," he said.

He said had the government wanted to keep the promise made in its election manifesto, it should have gone ahead and regularised slums erected till 2000, ensuring that all those within the new cut-off period got the benefit.

Shetty said the GR issued on the issue imposes conditions such as: the transfer of a hutment would only be carried out between two eligible slum-dwellers; both parties should be registered as voters prior to January 1, 1995; the buyer should not have any other hutment in his name in Mumbai; the buyer should not have claimed rehabilitation benefit (of a free house) on another hutment.

Shetty also demanded that millworkers, whose lives had been shattered by closure of mills, should get free houses and should not be asked to pay, as per the government's policy, 25 per cent of the cost of the houses.

Heading: On-duty fire tender rams bike, kills youth - Indian Express
Content:
Husband under interrogation; neighbours shocked

A 25-year-old woman was found murdered — with her infant daughter still cradled in her arms and her six-month-old son sleeping nearby— at MHADA Colony in Goregaon west, sending a shock wave through the colony.

The body of Shaheen was discovered by her maid on Friday morning. The maid frantically ran the bell of Shaheen's neighbour, 50-year-old Pupa Shekhar, who lives with her three teenaged daughters at Sai Samarth building in the colony.

Both the babies are alive.

Recounting her horror, she says, "At around 9:30 am, the maid who works for Shaheen rang my bell and told me that the door to Shaheen's house was ajar and there was something terrible inside. When I peeped in, I saw the body of Shaheen lying on a bed placed on the floor, in a pool of blood. Her daughter, one-and-a-half-year-old Shifa, was cradled in her arms. Shaheen has a son of six months, whose name we do not know yet. He was lying on a bed nearby."

Pupa immediately alerted other neighbours and the police were informed.

DCP Makarand Ranade (Zone 11) said, "When officers from Goregaon police station reached the spot, they discovered that the children were alive and had merely fallen asleep. The woman's body was taken to Cooper hospital for autopsy and the children will be sent to relatives of the mother as soon as we find them. The woman's husband, one Aslam Sheikh (35), a real estate agent was absconding. We suspect his hand in the murder. We traced him to Saki Naka and now he is in our custody. We are interrogating him to find whether he was responsible for the murder and where he had been since he left home on Thursday evening."

According to the neighbours, Shaheen was the second wife of Aslam and his first wife used to stay elsewhere in Mumbai, though they do not know the location. "Aslam did not stay in Shaheen's house all the time. He used to visit her twice or thrice a week and stay for the night. Apart from that, I do not know any relative or any family friends. Shaheen used to keep to herself though her daughter Shifa would sometimes come near our house and then Shaheen I would exchange a few words," said Pupa.

Pupa said Aslam and his wife have been staying in the rented flat for the past one-and-a-half-year.

Heading: Civic body, MHADA play blame game over Sayyed House collapse - Indian Express
Content:
Driver was on wrong side of street to reach fire site quickly, say police

A 22-year-old youth was killed on Friday after a fire tender coming from the wrong side rammed into the bike he was riding on Andheri Link Road near the D N Nagar police station. The youth, identified as Kailash Choudhari, died on the spot.

Police said that a fire was reported at the Horizon Hotel at near Juhu and the driver of the fire tender was trying to make his way through the wrong side of the street which he took to avoid the traffic on the other side.

According to the D N Nagar police, where the case is registered, Kailash, who hails from Rajasthan, had been working as a domestic cook and stayed in a slum at Kapaswadi with his brother Shankar (23) and a few other youths from their village. "Kailash was on his way towards Vile Parle on the Andheri Link Road on his bike when a fire engine coming in from the other direction rammed into him. Kailash fell from his bike right in the way of the vehicle, which ran over him, killing him instantly," said ACP Dilip Suryavanshi from the DN Nagar division.

The body has been sent to the Cooper Hospital for post-mortem.

The victim's brother Shankar, who had come to the police station, said, "We are four brothers, and our father does not work anymore. I have not yet informed my family members in Rajasthan about Kailash's death. But I will be taking his body to our village as soon as it is released." 

The vehicle's driver, Vijay Azarekar (50), has been arrested by the police. "It is quite clear that the driver was driving negligently as he was going on the wrong side of the street. Though there was a fire emergency at the hotel, the driver should have had taken precautions," said Suryavanshi.

When contacted, Chief Fire Officer Ajit Sawant said, "It is an unfortunate incident. The driver should have taken precautions. There have been cases like this before, when there is traffic and firemen cannot find way to reach the fire accident site. So they take it from the wrong side or lane. But our firemen and fire engines have also met with accidents¿ and some even died under private vehicles."

Heading: Businessman held for extorting money from friend - Indian Express
Content:
Two days after the Sayyed House collapse that killed six people, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation admitted that the entire fifth floor of the building was illegally constructed. The civic body, however, failed to give reason on why no action was taken till now. The BMC added that the piling work in the next plot was not the main cause for damage.

In a report on the collapse, the BMC has said that the fifth floor was unauthorised. "Not all unauthorised constructions can be demolished in a year's time. We are investigating whether MHADA had communicated to us to take action on the structure," said Municipal Commissioner, Jairaj Phatak. The MHADA, which was informed about the illegal construction in 1990, has said that the BMC was told to take action on the structure.

"We need to inspect the past records if any such letter was given to the BMC," Phatak said, adding, "We don't want to blame anyone but the ground reality needs to be checked."

MHADA in its report on the collapse has said that old age of the structure, additional alteration like illegal construction of floor, kitchen and toilet at the rear side and the piling work might have triggered the collapse.

Civic officials also said that while no communication from the residents of Sayyed House was recorded with the BMC on the piling work in the adjacent plot resulting into vibrations, there was one complaint from the builder, Rubberwala developers, to take action on the two illegal floors of the Sayyed House. "On July 5, 2007, the builder gave a complaint letter stating that Sayyed House has two illegal floors and is in a dilapidated condition and can collapse any time during monsoon. Inspection was carried by civic officials and the landowners agreed to demolish a room on the sixth floor which was being constructed then," said assistant municipal commissioner, B ward, S G Bhujbal.

Heading: Men-in-khaki organise a fun-filled Children’s Day in city - Indian Express
Content:
The Mumbai Police Crime Branch on Friday arrested a businessman who hatched a plan to extort several lakh rupees from a government servant who considered him his 'best friend'. The police also arrested an accomplice who had made the extortion calls to the victim.

The accused have been identified as Omar Sharif Abdul Gaffar Shaikh (35) and Naushad Hussain (25). They have been remanded to police custody till November 24.

"The complainant, a government servant, started receiving extortion threats from an anonymous caller in the first week of September. He was asked to pay up Rs 20 lakh and was threatened with dire consequences if he failed to do so. After this, he started receiving threats through SMS. Finally, on September 15, the complainant was given an ultimatum to pay the amount or face dire consequences," said Joint Commissioner of Police (Crime) Rakesh Maria.

The complainant negotiated the amount to Rs 17 lakh but could gather only Rs 14 lakh. He was directed to go to Nerul railway station and sit on a train headed for Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus. He set out with his best friend Omar Shaikh. On reaching Juinagar station, he was asked to get off and board the next train.

"The complainant got scared and asked Omar to follow the orders of the caller. On reaching a chosen spot between Sewri and Cotton Green stations, Omar threw the cash-filled bag out of the train," said Maria.

Four days after this, the complainant again received a call from the accused stating that only Rs 11.5 lakh had been found in the bag and he would now have to pay up an additional Rs 14 lakh. "The complainant then registered a case with the Anti Extortion Cell. A trap was laid at Gateway of India and Naushad, the caller, was arrested. He revealed that he had made the calls on the orders of Omar, who had planned the entire incident," said Maria.

Heading: Four held for extortion attempt - Indian Express
Content:
Once when a policeman thrashed 60-year-old Kalabai Pawar's four-year-old grandson rendering him unconscious, Pawar had opined that the 'heartless police force' does not deserve to have any children. However, the grandmother who continues to stay with her family on the footpath near Mafatlal Centre, could hardly suppress her tears on Friday, when she saw her grandson laughing gleefully after watching a magic show performed as part of Children's Day celebrations organised by the Zone I police.

On Friday morning, the Azad Maidan police hall was buzzing with the chatter of over 200 street children who were eagerly waiting for the magic show to start. The chatter soon turned into excited shrieks when they saw performers dressed in costumes of the characters from the latest Disney movie. After falling over each other to shake hands with the performers, the children hushed up for the magic show.

As the children gaped with wonder, their parents beamed. "In the 55 years of my life on the footpath near Mafatlal Centre we have been kicked out by the BMC and harassed by the police. However this is the first time when they have invited us here and done something for the children," said Pawar who sells flowers.

Joint Commissioner of Police, Law and Order K L Prasad and MP Supriya Sule praised the police force for successfully mixing fun with purpose. NGOs also attended the event and showed a keenness to work with the police for children's welfare.

"An interaction between the police and the NGOs is necessary for furthering the cause of these children. For this purpose we will be listing the names of such children in our police stations and the NGOs interested in working with them can contact us," said Deputy Commissioner of Police, Zone I, Vishwas Nangre-Patil. For the children, the celebrations were akin to Diwali, Christmas and New Year festivities. Six-year-old Swapna Rane, who lives with her parents in Fort market said, "They told us that it's a day for children to enjoy and learn at the same time. The lady from the NGO told us to go to school and not beg. The magic show was the best thing in the programme."

Dr Smita Dharmamer who works with Aangan, an NGO that gives counseling to those who are in constant conflict with the law, said that the organisation will ensure that the children receive opportunities for education. "We intend to counsel both the parents and the children about the importance of education and will also help them register in schools," she said.

Heading: Susairaj’s bail plea adjourned - Indian Express
Content:
The Mumbai Police Crime Branch on Thursday arrested four notorious history-sheeters who allegedly attempted to extort Rs 10 lakh from a tenant after he was given Rs 15 lakh by his landlord as part of an out-of-court settlement.

The arrested accused have been identified as Deepak Walekar alias Pandav Putra, Ramesh Junghare, Ganesh Suryavanshi alias Gonya, and Kiran Wagle alias Kiran Bhajiwala. They were arrested by Unit 2 of the Crime Branch and have been remanded to police custody till November 21.

"Deepak Walekar is a former Arun Gawli gang member who has been running his own gang, known as 'the Pandav Putra gang', for some time. He was arrested for the first time in 1993 and has 17 serious offences previously registered against him at Kherwadi, Girgaum and DB Marg police stations among others. He was given the name Pandav Putra owing to his diminutive size and the manner in which he once attempted to evade arrest by dressing up in a school boy's uniform and carrying a school-bag," said Joint Commissioner of Police (Crime) Rakesh Maria.

According to the police, the complainant in the case is a tenant who took a godown on hire in 2002. In 2006, he got into a dispute with the owner of the godown and the matter was taken to court. In August this year, both parties reached an out-of-court settlement by way of which the complainant received Rs 15 lakh to clear out.

"The accused got wind of this and when the complainant was in court for some work Junghare and Gonya cornered him in a corridor and demanded that he pay them Rs 10 lakh. When he refused, they threatened him with dire consequences," said Maria.

Junghare has six previous cases registered against him, while Gonya has four offences against his name. Except for Wagle, who has one prior offence against his name, all the arrested accused have cases registered against them under the stringent Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act.

Heading: Robber traced using only fingerprints - Indian Express
Content:
The Bombay High Court on Friday adjourned the hearing of the bail application moved by Kannada actress Maria Monica Susairaj, accused in the murder of TV executive Neeraj Grover case, till Wednesday.

Maria has moved the court for bail, pleading not guilty for the murder charges slapped against her. According to her application, there is nothing to prove her motive behind the murder and there is no evidence to sustain the murder charges against her.

According to her lawyer G S Kannur, this is a fit case for granting bail.

The application also states that there is no possibility of tampering with the evidence.

The sessions court on September 16 had rejected her bail plea for the second time on the grounds that prima facie evidence was available in the case against Maria and her naval officer fiancé and co-accused, Emile Jerome Mathew.

The court had rejected defence's plea of making Maria an accused only in the part pertaining to destruction of evidence. The defence had said that the murder was not pre-mediated as Susairaj had called Mathew 20 times from her mobile on May 6, the night of the incident pleading him to come to Mumbai.

Despite Susairaj's statement that she was party only to the destruction of evidence, the police in June named her as the main accused who had engineered the crime.

Heading: Two held for snatching chains, bags - Indian Express
Content:
The MRA Marg police along with Mumbai police's Fingerprints Bureau have arrested a man for his role in a robbery at a Sony Ericsson showroom. What was unique about the arrest was the fact that the investigators only had the culprit's fingerprints as clue.

One Tabrej Abu Ansari (24) and his accomplice broke into the Sony Ericsson showroom in Ravi building at DN Road on the night of October 17. They stole 19 cameras and 100 mobile phones worth Rs 10, 75,000. A case was registered at the MRA Marg police station following which the police and the officers of the Fingerprints Bureau thoroughly investigated the scene of crime and found latent fingerprints on walls and doors of cabinets. The fingerprints were found to match with Ansari's, taken by the Bureau for a motorbike theft case in Agripada.

The investigators found that Ansari was a resident of Nagpada. On Thursday he was arrested from his residence. 27 mobile phones and 14 cameras worth Rs 3,85,646 were also recovered. Ansari's accomplice, who the police did not wish to name, is still at large.

Ansari will be produced in a magistrate's court on Friday when the police will seek his custody.

"This has been an excellent piece of detection work by the Fingerprints Bureau," said DCP Vishwas Nangre-Patil of Zone 1.

"This is a very rare case of detection since it is very difficult to catch criminals in house breaking cases by fingerprints alone. In other robbery cases we usually have descriptions to work on but the fingerprints were all we had this time," he added.

The fingerprints have made MRA police's case stronger, "We can know convict him without any problems. There's no denying fingerprint evidence in court," said Police Inspector R Doiphode of MRA Marg police station.

Heading: Teens held for stealing TV to buy alcohol - Indian Express
Content:
A special squad formed by DCP Makarand Ranade of Zone 11, to curb incidents of chain and bag snatching on Link Road in the Bangur Nagar jurisdiction, nabbed two youths early this month for their involvement in six cases of chain snatching, five cases of bag snatching and one case of burglary.

According to the police, the duo hail from respectable families and have been snatching chains and bags to make easy money. They used to spend the money on expensive dining and alcohol.

DCP Makarand Ranade (Zone 11) said, "For the past 2-3 months, we have been noticing an increase in incidents of bag and chain snatching in our zone, especially in the area between Evershine Nagar and Bhagat Singh Nagar. To nab the accused, a special team was formed which patrolled the area and gathered information in plain clothes so as to avoid any suspicion."

After conducting enquiries, the police team learnt that a youth identified as Ayaz Merchant (22) and his accomplice were responsible for most of the incidents of chain and bag snatching in the area.

"Based on the information, early on November 6, our team nabbed Merchant from the Link Road while he was targeting joggers in the area," said Ranade.

During interrogation, Merchant revealed the details of his accomplice, identified as Zahid Ahmed Khan (19), who was then arrested.

The police recovered chains, mobile phones and cash to the tune of Rs 2, 78,500 from the duo. "The two are in police custody till November 15," added Ranade.

Heading: The show goes on - Indian Express
Content:
The RCF police have arrested two 19-year-olds for stealing a TV set from their neighbour's flat and selling it for Rs 1,000 to buy alcohol. According to the police, the accused—Digambar More and Aneez Shaik—were alcoholics. While More worked as a waiter, Shaikh worked in a fish market. "A couple of months back, when the duo returned to their building, they found that a room on their floor was locked. They broke into the room and stole a television set. They then allegedly sold it for Rs 1000 and bought alcohol from the money," said Assistant Police Inspector Rajesh Kewale of the RCF police station.

"We received a tip off from a source who claimed to have seen the duo with the television set. After we nabbed them, they confessed to having stolen the TV and selling it," said Kewale.

Heading: Flick the switch - Indian Express
Content:
Why reruns will always charm Indian viewers

Way back in the early days of cable television, teens and tweens used to obsessively watch the adventures of a young boy called Kevin Arnold. The Wonder Years is only one of the shows that the first cable-TV generation of India remembers with fondness and there was collective heartbreak when it aired its final episode.

Right now, reruns are the flavour of the season; a rather forced scenario given the frequent strikes in the television industry. Anupama Mandloi, Senior Creative Director at Star Plus, is a little skeptical about how long reruns will engage the interest of viewers. "There is a limit to which the viewers will continue watching the same shows repeatedly. It is an unfortunate situation where we are forced to replay new and old re-runs since all productions are at standstill."

But reruns are not a new phenomenon forced by the strike; some of the most popular ones —Friends, Seinfeld, Sex and the City— have been airing for ages. And recently, some shows like The Wonder Years, Beverly Hills 90210 and The

X-Files have come back on air, running in Zee Café's Old Skool slot. Neil Chakravarti, Business Head of Zee Café says that the slot was started because there was a yearning among viewers to revisit some old classics. "The audiences in the 25-34 age-group wanted to relive the memories whereas the younger, teenage viewers wished to get a glimpse of the classic shows that they keep reading about," he explains, "So, it was two distinct set of viewers who were interested in watching the show —though for different reasons."

However, the list of re-telecast shows includes some continuing franchises like Grey's Anatomy, Desperate Housewives and The Oprah Winfrey Show. Chakravarti explains this by saying, "Viewer requests form the biggest reason for these shows."

Reruns of Indian shows have not met with the same success. Some of the few rerun successes are Dekh Bhai Dekh, Sarabhai vs Sarabhai and Hum Log. Swabhimaan, one of the most popular soaps on Indian television till date is also very popular as a rerun. Rohit Roy, who played the iconic Rishabh Malhotra on the show says, "A show will run successfully in its rerun stage only if it connects with the audience," he says. Tanaaz Irani, who played Babli on the same show, is of the opinion that the most important reason for the continuing success of old shows is that they remain fresh. "We really worked hard at getting the right shots," she says, "Now TV shows are shot in a hurry and they're canned in one take."

How much does nostalgia account for the popularity of reruns? Mandloi is not sure that it is a deciding factor. "People are constantly on the lookout for some thing fresh, contemporary and top of mind. The only content that has nostalgia value is really reruns of movies and even there the more current the better," she says. Chakravarti disagrees, "Nostalgia is one factor that we spotted early. It has worked positively for us and we are enthused to continue doing so as the viewers expect such initiatives from us now."

One thing is certain, nostalgia or strike, the season of reruns will never end on Indian television and we're mighty glad about that.

Heading: TALKING POINT with Chunky Pandey - Indian Express
Content:
Chicks on Flicks
Sony PIX
Friday, 7:30 pm
Rating**
What's it about? When Chicks on Flicks was announced, one must admit, it seemed like a good idea. We have had various men on TV, from the legendary Tom Brooks of BBC's Talking Movies, to our own home-grown movie critic Rajeev Masand telling us what movie to watch and what to avoid. Chicks on Flicks, for a change, has two women talking about movies and Hollywood movies, at that. This is not just a film review show; there are also interview segments where you see, for the first time, Indian TV show hosts interacting with the A-list of Hollywood.

Who's in it? The show is hosted by actor Ira Dubey and model Neha Sareen. About their qualifications to host a show of this type, we'll say very little. But the best that can be said about them is that they do seem to be trying really hard to keep it light and engaging. What does not help is the almost-zero chemistry between the two and the fact that they seem to be taking their label as 'Hollywood Film Critic' a bit too seriously. A few tongue-in-cheek jokes and some laughter on the sets wouldn't hurt, girls.

What's hot? The best thing about the show is that it lasts only half-hour. The pilot episode about the latest Bond movie, Quantum of Solace, was interesting enough, mainly because the girls managed to get interviews with Daniel Craig and Olga Kurylenko, and director Marc Forster. But will they be able to sustain the same level of interest for a movie that's not as popular as the Bond franchise?

What's not? The hosts seem very uncomfortable before the camera. The promos and initial trailers of the show projected an image that seemed like mix of Sex and the City and Talking Movies. The real product does not quite live up to that promise. It lacks the chutzpah of SATC and the pure cerebral value of Talking Movies. Moreover, the moments of interaction between the two hosts seem forced and unnatural. You get the impression that they'd rather be talking to the camera than to each other.

Should you be watching it? Watch the show if and only if you're completely clueless about what to expect from the latest Hollywood releases.

For those more clued into the movie scene, we suggest you give this show a miss and watch the movies and form your own judgements.

Heading: Tondulkar adjudged best - Indian Express

Through its popular shows such as Doraremon, Kiteretsu and Kochikame or through its wacky Pyjama Pakdo contests, Hungama has established itself as a destination that encourages kids to be themselves. Now it takes the laughter on-ground, with its biggest event ever - Mahachoco presents Mission Ha Ha Hungama— at MMRDA Grounds, Bandra on November 29. Kids will be egged on to laugh out loud through a hilarious stage performance where Doraemon, Shinchan along with Darsheel Safary will enthrall kids with their acts.

He was very cooperative and patient with us. He did not mind if we goofed our lines and had to give a take once again". Shahid's cutesy appeal seems to be attracting the kids as well.

Reality check
So far the viewers have seen their favourite couples perform on the stage and entertain the audience with their various dance forms.

But this time around it is the exciting off-stage drama of the pairs that is going to take centre stage on this dance reality show. The reality episodes of Nach Baliye 4 will make the audience privy to all the fun, laughter, happenings, tension in the rehearsal halls, the tiffs with their choreographers and all that toil that goes behind the scenes. Here's a chance to finally get real.

Cause and effect

The actor recently played a charity Cricket Match, in support of the cause of Beti, a campaign against female foeticide. Heading: The more things change - Indian Express
Content:
Prasoon Joshi talks about his songs in Ghajini and how interfering Aamir Khan really is

In the film industry, everyone is on song. Even if it is a shaven, tattooed Aamir Khan who can't remember his phone number. Little wonder, Prasoon Joshi found himself penning poetry for all the brawn and brawl on display in Ghajini. "It is a fast-paced thriller with a lot of action and high energy, but the songs are extremely important to the narrative," says Joshi who has written five songs, all composed by A R Rahman, for the Khan starrer.

The film is a remake of a Tamil movie that was released three years ago, with songs written by N Muthukumar, but Joshi says the Hindi soundtrack is completely original. "I did not even listen to the southern version as I did not want to be influenced in anyway," says Joshi, who, however, watched bits of the film to "gather a feel of it".

A little-known fact about ad man Joshi is that he is a trained classical musician who likes to compose and sing as well, but he has given them a miss in Ghajini.

"I think it is very important for a lyricist to have a sense of music since it's then that the song shapes up wholly," says Joshi. He has composed and sung jingles for Alpenliebe and Happy Dent, among others. "But it's not something I'd do for films," he says.

Bollywood has heard enough complaints of Aamir Khan's interference, but Joshi thinks otherwise. "He is a very intelligent man and when he has a suggestion, it's often valid. When it is not, we argue a lot and whoever has a more powerful logic wins. So I'd say there's close understanding and mutual respect that allow us to bounce ideas off each other," he says.

If Joshi's poetry is not enough, then maybe you can watch the songs for another reason — one of them has Khan sporting six different hairstyles. Guess it's all relevant to the narrative.

Heading: Seeing Stars - Indian Express
Content:
It seems the American flag just got another colour. The colour purple. Or is it the colour toffee? And as my television set bears witness to the sight of a new history, to the sights and sounds of wild celebration, to the tears in the streets of New York and Chicago, I cannot help but wonder: Is this really change?

Has the world really shifted on its axis? Has the black man finally wrenched himself free? Will the economy miraculously right itself? Will the war in Iraq really end? Or is the only real change in our hearts? And in our minds, desperately clawing at fragile straws of good news?

In my home we have a new maid. That change seems real enough. Especially since she is a live-in. But my nine year old daughter seems to be uncomfortable. "Why does she sleep on a mattress on the floor, when I sleep on top of the bed?" she asked plaintively. "If I had to sleep on the floor and someone else slept on top of the bed I would feel like crying," she said to my wife and her mother, breaking our hearts with her earnestness.

How can I tell her that this is probably a better life than anything our new maid is accustomed to? Or is it? Is she less equal in her own hut, in her own village, among her own people, sleeping presumably happily on a cow dung floor? Or does she prefer air-conditioning to equality? On the road outside my house, more change.

The other day a large orange and green, political looking poster, with many smiling photographs, proclaimed with what I am sure is justifiable pride, that our corporator had actually managed to start the process of cement concreting our street. The next day a corrugated tin barricade separated the road into two neat halves and traffic honked untidily in all directions trying to get its head around the new obstacle. A small sign caught my eye.

It said quietly that the aforementioned cement concreting would be complete by 2011.

2011?!! Are you flickin' crazy? I mean 2011 is the year that comes after 2010 and way after 2009 and in case nobody noticed, we are still only approaching the end of 2008.

And then of course there is the financial newspaper that is stuffed into my door handle everyday. Whose headlines have changed alarmingly southward in just three or four months. And there are images on TV of people being beaten mercilessly for one reason and another. And of course there is the small matter of Hindus no longer seeming to be clashing with Muslims but preferring to fight with other Hindus instead. This is change.

As also the fact that we are finally beating the Aussies. At cricket and at sledging, that artful bye-product of the gentleman's game, a bye-product that they so proudly developed virtually single-handedly.

And while still on cricket, we seem to be on the cusp of generations. The door is open both ways, for the old guard walking nobly out into the sunset, as well as for the young strong eager hearts galloping in to do battle for pride and country.

Meanwhile my little dog Atom is learning to pee with his leg up. He hasn't quite got it yet and gender identity might still be an issue but we shall see. And as my morning coffee grows cold and stale, the noises on the street tell me that we are heading for a new election of our own.

But in a certain way, the scenes outside my window are still unchanging. The faces pressed against the glass looking in at me with eager greed, clamouring already for those few precious drops of voter's ink, are still the same.

And I see in their eyes what I have seen before: No hope. Only audacity.

(Contact the columnist on adipochas@yahoo.com)
