But not all of them are ordinary civilians fleeing from war; some could have connections with LTTE, some could even be cadres themselves. From a security perspective, it is necessary that we scan their past and monitor their activities," said a police officer.

Heading: Karuna to Centre: don’t be fooled by Lankan sweet-talk - Indian Express
Content:
There has been widespread infighting in the ranks of both the Congress and BJP over the distribution of tickets for the Rajasthan assembly elections. This is most evident in tribal dominated south Rajasthan, where rebel candidates have decided to contest against both parties in 20 out of the 28 constituencies.

The Congress seems to have the larger problem. It has had to bear the brunt of rebels in 18 seats, while the BJP faces protests in six constituencies. But senior leaders fear this could increase, following problems with heavyweights like Bharatpur MP Vishvendra Singh and Meena leader, Kirori Lal Meena.

With Congress rebels contesting in seven of Udaipur district's nine constituencies alone, the Pradesh Congress Committee (PCC) has sent special AICC observers to the City of Lakes to try and stem the mutiny. Meanwhile, local BJP leaders have put their campaigns momentarily on hold to pacify rebels.

The Congress rebellion reached its zenith last week when Rajasthan Congress secretary Vinay Tyagi walked out of the party after being denied a ticket from the Mavli constituency. "Ticket allotment in this entire region was all wrong barring a few of the 28 candidates. Most are undeserving while those who have worked to promote the party even under the BJP's tyrannical rule these five years were sidelined," he said.

Incidentally, with a dominant tribal population, south Rajasthan had long remained a Congress bastion up to the Ashok Gehlot-led Congress regime in 1998, when the Congress won 28 of the 30 seats. A strong anti-Gehlot sentiment and rebellion in a few seats in 2003 gave the BJP the upper hand, helping it to sweep 23 of the 30 constituencies. The number of constituencies in the region was brought down to 28 by the delimitation exercise ahead of the 2008 polls. Congress leaders say that south Rajasthan was always the region the party banked on to form the government in past elections.

BJP leader from Udaipur, Anil Singhal admits that there are disgruntled party workers and candidates. "Party workers in Dungarpur and Banswada districts are unhappy about candidates selected there as they believe they are not from a BJP background. We are working hard to pacify these rebels and bring them back to the party line," says Singhal.

Heading: Milk deaths: parents block road, fume at missing Soren - Indian Express
Content:
Warning the Centre against being "fooled by the sweet-talk" of the Sri Lankan Government, Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M Karunanidhi told the Assembly on Friday that the DMK members were ready to resign from power if that would press the Centre to take measure to protect the Tamils in Sri Lanka.

"President Mahinda Rajapaksa has separated the Tigers of LTTE (whom they consider as terrorists) and other Tamils citizens of the country as two separate entities. While maintaining that Tigers were terrorists and would be put down accordingly, the Government there do not distinguish between innocent Tamils and LTTE members," he said in the Assembly on the last day of the session.

Rejecting the latest ceasefire offer by LTTE, Rajapaksa has stated on the sidelines of a regional summit in Delhi on Thursday that while the rebels would be dealt as terrorists till they put down their arms, the Tamil families would not be harmed in anyway.

"Rajapaksa said in Delhi that innocent Tamils will not be harmed in anyway. This is mere sweet-talk indulged by the Lankan President to fool the Tamils here. The Centre should understand the real intention behind this talk," the CM said.

"If the rebels are considered as terrorists, it is for the Lankan Government and Army to decide on the ways to tackle the problem. But the armed forces should stop bombing innocent Tamils, their houses, streets, hamlets and villages. Rajapaksa is not willing to take that responsibility. The bombs being rained on the innocent Tamils in Lanka are the same explosives dropped on the Tigers. We realise that the Lankan Government is trying to eliminate all the Tamils in the name of fighting terrorism," Karunanidhi charged.

Many countries like India, Pakistan, the US and UK face the menace of terrorism but none of these countries drop shells on their own citizens in the pretext of fighting terror, he said, urging Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to convey this to Rajapaksa.

Karunanidhi also cautioned the Centre against being fooled by the assurances made by Rajapaksa in guaranteeing the safety of Tamils caught in the war, and said that India should strongly demand for a political solution to the decades-old conflict.

Heading: Phone tapping: panel for action against scribes in scandal, TN Govt says no - Indian Express
Content:
On Children's Day, a group of children squatted on the highway here, mourning friends who are no more. Parents and neighbours despaired no one from the Government had spoken to them. The rage of the community found expression in a daylong bandh in the block, which, however, was unaccompanied by violence.

Late last evening, five young boys died after drinking "poisonous milk" served to them at the Adivasi Awasiya Vidyalaya run by the Welfare Department of the Jharkhand government in Bedo, 30 km from state capital Ranchi. Jugeshwar Sahu, superintendent of the hostel, consumed the same milk, and is now admitted to the Rajendra Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS) hospital in Ranchi, along with 38 other children.

The boarding school has been shut indefinitely. A police cordon has been thrown around it. The Government declared a holiday in all schools in the district to mourn the deaths. All shops and business establishment in Bedo block remained shut. The blockade on the highway was lifted in the afternoon after SP (Rural) Kuldip Trivedi intervened. "There was no incident of violence anywhere," Trivedi said.

Hours after the deaths, Bedo Block Welfare Officer Vishwanath Sahu lodged a complaint against school headmaster Kelment Tigga, superintendent Sahu, cook Jagat and milk supplier Sarita, holding them responsible for the tragedy. All of them have been booked under Sections 304 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) and 328 (causing hurt by means of poison) IPC, but no one had been arrested till evening on Friday.

Samples of the milk were sent to Ranchi's Forensic Science Laboratory last night. "After we receive the report we will let you know," SSP M S Bhatia told The Indian Express.

The families of the dead and ill children were camping at RIMS. "Passions are running high, as many of the 38 students who were admitted last night have not recovered fully," RIMS director N N Agrawal said. "We shifted 10 children who were critically ill to Apollo Hospital."

Jharkhand Minister for Human Resources Bandhu Tirkey was mobbed by angry relatives at the hospital. At Bedo, parents shouted slogans against CM Shibu Soren. "I am shocked that our Chief Minister has no time for us," said Soma Oraon, father of Vineet, a Class VI student who was among the dead children. A parent who had been charged by policemen for trying to block the highway at Bedo, wept: "Nobody is ready to talk to us.We will withdraw our children from this school."

Heading: One campaign into five - Indian Express
Content:
A judicial inquiry commission that looked into two phone tapping controversies that rocked Tamil Nadu a few months ago has recommended legal proceedings against five journalists in its report tabled in the Assembly on Friday. However, the Government rejected the recommendation, said CM M Karunanidhi, adding that departmental action would be taken against the Government officials involved in the controversies.

The state Government had constituted a Commission of Inquiry, headed by retired Madras High Court Justice P Shanmugam, to probe into the controversies that broke out when conversations between state Social Welfare Minister Dr Poongothai Aladi Aruna and Vigilance Director S K Upadhyay were made public. The recorded conversation had the minister requesting the official to go easy on her relative, a junior government official with the Electricity Department caught on charges of accepting a bribe. The other tapping controversy also involved the same official. Even as the DMK made the minister put in her papers, the Commission was set up to probe how these two conversations were recorded and subsequently leaked to the media.

Heading: Judge examines Pandey, dismisses torture charges - Indian Express
Content:
The Congress party's Madhya Pradesh unit is that rare political entity that has spokespersons for different factions. Commerce Minister and Lok Sabha MP from Chhindwara, Kamal Nath, former chief minister Digvijay Singh, PCC chief Suresh Pachauri, Union minister of state and Lok Sabha MP from Guna Jyotiraditya Scindia, and HRD Minister Arjun Singh's son Ajay Singh represent the major factions in the party.

In keeping with the Congress thumb rule of not projecting a chief ministerial candidate, the party has officially not projected anyone to lead the campaign. Each leader, however, seems to have carved out a piece of the state for himself.

Kamal Nath was quickest off the block in Chhindwara. Incidentally, he was instrumental in bringing all factions together on his home turf by organising a 'Unity Show' recently but it ended up as a bid to project him as a contender for the top job. Scindia, who clearly has age and charisma on his side, began in Gwalior only on Wednesday. While Digvijay Singh has opted out of the contest, Nath, Scindia and Pachauri are MPs.

The only faction leader in the fray is Ajay Singh, who is also the campaign committee chairman. He is busy campaigning in Churhat in Sidhi district. The party came out with its chargesheet against the ruling party only on Wednesday.

The Congress claims there is a strategy behind going slow. "We don't want to invite national leaders before the tempo begins and make them stare at empty spaces like the BJP did," says Congress leader Brijmohan Srivastava.

Heading: CAG doubts official date on job scheme - Indian Express
Content:
Mahant Amritanand alias Dayanand Pandey, arrested from Kanpur in connection with the September 29 Malegaon blast and suspected by the Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad to be the prime conspirator in the case, today denied all allegations against him when he was produced in a Nashik court, and accused the police of torturing him.

"Mera naam Dayanand Pandey nahin hai (My name is not Dayanand Pandey)," was the first thing the mahant told the judge. To which Special Public Prosecutor Ajay Misar said: "Sir, the accused has a lot of names and Pandey is one of them."

Asked by Judge H K Ganatra if he had any complaints against the police, Pandey, dressed in a cream kurta-pyjama with his head covered with a black cloth, said: "I have been assaulted by the ATS since they took me into custody."

When Ganatra asked Pandey to show him physical marks on his body if that was the case, Pandey said the investigators had been clever and had tortured him in such a way that there were no external physical injuries. The judge then took Pandey to his chamber, personally examined him, and dismissed the torture charges.

Defence lawyer A K Chhallani, appearing for Pandey, argued that the ATS was using third-degree methods to draw a link and prove the false allegations levelled against Pandey. He also referred to the application moved by family members of Lt Col Prasad Purohit alleging torture in police custody.

However, the court said the allegations made by Pandey were baseless and asked the ATS to go by the law. The court also sought the consent of Pandey to conduct forensic tests on him. "If the court feels by conducting the test the truth will come out then I am ready for any test," Pandey said, after which he was remanded to police custody until November 26.

Heading: ‘Every time a blast takes place his name crops up...’ - Indian Express
Content:
Despite some "improvement" after the first reality check of National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREG) pointed to "significant deficiencies" in its implementation, the CAG has now expressed "serious doubts" over the reliability of official data as it could not be checked with ground level records.

"The scrutiny revealed that while there was a definite improvement in record maintenance, especially in Uttar Pradesh, after the conduct of the initial audit, the maintenance of basic records at the gram panchayat level, in particular the employment register, was still deficient and there was considerable scope for improvement. Further, the reliability of Monthly Progress Reports (MPRs) from the block and district levels was in serious doubt, as they could not be reconciled with the relevant basic records," the CAG has observed in its final performance audit re port for implementation of NREG. The observation has come after it revisited two-dozen blocks in 12 districts of six states from the original 68 districts audited in February-March this year.

The CAG's observation regarding the unreliability of official data holds significance in view of the fact that the UPA Government has been trumpeting NREG performance, using the record employment generation from its official data compiled using MPRs.

While the CAG pointed improvement by Uttar Pradesh in the 'limited scrutiny' for record maintenance, the performance of West Bengal, Bihar, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan were found lacking on several counts. That the mess cuts across parties and states is evident from CAG's findings.

The CAG's findings after 'limited scrutiny' of record maintenance follows the six-month performance audit of the NREGS in 513 gram panchayats spread across 68 randomly selected districts between May and September last year. The Indian Express had first reported about the startling revelations about deficiencies in the implementation of NREG compiled in the draft performance audit report this January.

The findings

• Excess reporting of 6.06 lakh mandays of cumulative employment in Purulia district

• Excess reporting of fund utilisation of Rs 0.99 crore in West Midnapore and Purulia districts of West Bengal

• Excess reporting of expenditure of Rs 174.29 lakh in Maharashtra

• No photograph was affixed on 1,093 job cards issued to the registered households in two blocks of Maharashtra

• In all four blocks surveyed in Jharkhand, no photograph was affixed in any of the 3,189 job cards

• In Bihar, no photographs were affixed in job card registers

• In Rajasthan, in one block in Udaipur district, no records were available in support of the block level reports of half the gram panchayats

Heading: Congress alleges SIMI-Sangh links, seeks task force probe - Indian Express
Content:
Every year since his son had left home in 2001 on the day of Eid, he sits near the telephone, waiting for him to call. And when the calls come he and his wife talk for over an hour. This year too, he waited. But no call came.

But Ishaq Ali Khan, father of Amir Reza Khan who has been accused in several cases of terror attacks in India, including the attack on American Center in 2002, has not lost hope.

"I am sure he will call on Bakr-Eid," 62-year old Ishaq, who runs a business in building materials, told The Indian Express, sitting in his Beniapukur home in central Kolkata.

Apart from his alleged involvement in the American Center attack, Amir has also been accused of being involved in the abduction of Kolkata shoe merchant Partha Roy Burman in 2001. He was one of the seven who had been served with a death sentence in the American Center attack case. And it's he and Hasan Imam who still elude the police.

Only last week Mohammed Sadiq alias Sadaqat, who shot dead six cops in the American Center attack, was caught by the Mumbai police.

Amir, according to the police, is the head of the Indian Mujahideen, suspected to be behind the recent serial blasts across the country.

Ishaq says he gets scared whenever a blast takes place.

"Every time a blast takes place his name crops up. When the Assam blasts took place, I got scared thinking that his name would come up. He is touted as the head of Indian Mujahideen but let me tell you, he never cared even for his mohallah. He was quite an introvert. How can a person like him head an all-Indian organisation?" he asked.

Ishaq Ali Khan stays with his wife Hasina Khanam. He had five sons —- Asif Reza Khan who was also involved in the abduction of Partha Roy Burman and was later shot dead by Gujarat Police when he allegedly tried to flee from them in 2001; Ali Reza Khan, a real estate developer; Amir Reza who, police suspect, is in Pakistan now; Imran Reza Khan, a businessman and Ehtasam Reza Khan, a student.

At present, only the elderly couple stay at their Beniapukur house. Their sons have settled down in different parts of the city and all his five daughters have been married off. When Amir called last year, Ishaq had asked why he committed such a crime (the attack on the American Center).

"But my son said he was staying in Dubai and denied his involvement in any crime. He said he was engaged in business there," the elderly man said. He also said that he had no complaints against the police. "They never created trouble for me. They never disturbed me," Ishaq said.

He said he had told Amir's wife that she had the liberty to get married again. "Amir cannot come back. His wife and daughter have gone back to her parental home in Lucknow.

Heading: Pak player injured, mother dies watching live telecast - Indian Express
Content:
Suggesting linkages between the Indian Mujahideen/ SIMI and organisations affiliated to the Sangh Parivar, the Congress on Friday demanded that Government of India should set up a Multi-Disciplinary Task Force to conduct a detailed investigation into the "various dimensions". It also demanded an inquiry by a judge of the Supreme Court to see if organisations like Sankalp and private military schools were trying to subvert the neutrality of the "government structure" of the country.

"Evidence in public space indicates that they (IM/ SIMI and those allegedly affiliated to the Sangh Parivar) could be linked somewhere. If outsourcing happened in one case, why can't it be in other cases?" said AICC spokesperson Manish Tewari.

Human Resource Development Minister Arjun Singh termed the party's demands as "good suggestions" adding that the approach should be "non-partisan". Asked if he agreed to the party's suggestion of links between IM/SIMI and those affiliated to the Sangh Parivar, he said, "You may call it pre-conceived but I have always had doubts about the Sangh Parivar. This was brought up immediately after Mahatma Gandhi's assassination but it was not taken up then."

Accusing the Gujarat Government of trying to "suppress" the investigations into Modasa blasts, Tewari said investigating officer of the case had gone to the extent of giving a clean chit to Pragya Thakur and her associates despite the fact that similarities between Modasa and Malegaon blasts could not be more glaring.

Heading: The K-deal - Indian Express
Content:
The five-match India-Pakistan Kabaddi tournament organised on the occasion of 300th Guruta Gaddi Diwas celebrations ended on a tragic note on Friday after the mother of Pakistani raider Akhtar Pathan died of a heart attack while watching the live telecast of the match in Pakistan. The match was being telecast live on PTC Punjabi channel.

Pathan had sustained a serious leg injury during one of the raids and there were repeated announcements for bringing the ambulance inside the ground to take him for treatment. "She (Pathan's mother) thought that Pathan had sustained some life threatening injury and that was why ambulance was being called. Shocked, she suffered a heart attack and passed away," Pakistan coach Zafar Ahmad Bhatti told The Indian Express late on Friday. "After the match was over, we received a phone call from his brother in Pakistan," he added.

It was learnt that Pathan was not immediately told about the tragic incident.

Pathan, a livewire raider of the Pakistani team, had only one unsuccessful raid on Friday in which he got seriously injured and had trouble walking. However, displaying true sportsman spirit, he decided to

have another go. In his last raid, Pathan came back successful, only to fall on the ground suddenly. Pathan, who was seen writing in pain,

was assisted by teammates. Despite his heroics, the Pakistani team eventually lost to India 28 points to 35.

Heading: Selectors may rest Zaheer - Indian Express
Content:
The Board of Control for Cricket in India on Friday decided to move the Supreme Court challenging the Calcutta High Court's directive to initiate criminal proceedings against six top officials for filing false affidavits in the Jagmohan Dalmiya expulsion case.

After consulting top lawyers since Wednesday's development, the BCCI has gone through the papers and will move the Supreme Court soon.

"It was an ex parte order and the BCCI officials were not given an opportunity to put across their case. We have decided to move the Supreme Court in this matter", BCCI's finance committee chairman Rajiv Shukla said on Friday.

The Calcutta High Court on Wednesday directed initiation of criminal proceedings against BCCI President Sashank Manohar, former board president Sharad Pawar and four top officials for filing false affidavits in the Dalmiya expulsion case.

The six BCCI officials, against whom criminal proceedings are to be initiated, have been asked not to speak on the issue since the matter was sub-judice. "Since our lawyers are handling the issue, it is better to allow them to do their work and not complicate matters by making public statements," an official said.

Heading: Hurting Yuvi inflicts pain - Indian Express
Content:
With medium-pacer Ishant Sharma forced to sit out of the first one-day international against England in Rajkot due to an ankle sprain, the Indian selection committee is taking no chances with Zaheer Khan.

It has been learnt that the committee, headed by K Srikkanth, will give Mumbai pacer Zaheer a break. The left-armer has been bowling continuously over the last couple of months. The two pacers had bowled a combined 276 overs in the four-Test series against Australia before getting a three-day break ahead of the England ODIs.

Zaheer had skipped India's first net practice in Rajkot and only had a light training session on the eve of the match. On Friday, Zaheer bowled a splendid spell of 7-126-3 which saw key wickets of England's Ian Bell, Owais Shah and Andrew Flintoff.

"We don't want Zaheer to injure himself the way Ishant did," says a selector on condition of anonymity. "There is lot of cricket ahead and we need his services for the Test series as he is our main strike bowler. We can't afford to lose him. But a lot also depends on how the first three matches go."

With Munaf Patel and RP Singh in the squad, the selector feels it's a good time for the fast bowler to take a break. "RP and Munaf have been in squad and have not played too much cricket. We have won today and if we continue our form, we could give him a break," selector added.

The first Test is scheduled to be played from December 11-15 in Ahmedabad.

Heading: Return of the Singh - Indian Express
Content:
A glance at the scoreboard told only half the tale. It was the story behind the numbers that was far more interesting as India thumped England by 158 runs in the first one-day international on Friday. Consider this, for example: the Indian batsmen scored 230 runs in boundaries (38 fours and 13 sixes), the visitors scored 229 runs in all.

It was a kind of game that comes along every once in a while — one team gets everything right, the other needs a scanner to find any positives to take away from it.

Once England were set a mammoth 388 to chase, it seemed certain that they would give up long before the final lap. A couple of partnerships, and skipper Kevin Pietersen's 56-ball 63, ensured they survived till the 38th over, but the result was never in doubt.

Wrong decision

It had all started going wrong for the visitors in the morning. Pietersen won the toss but was fooled into believing that the greenish tinge on the pitch would provide early help to his bowlers. He put the Indians in, and after that first faulty step, it was all downhill.

There was a 100-plus opening stand between Virender Sehwag and Gautam Gambhir, a confident 43 by one-drop Suresh Raina, a savage 78-ball 138 (with 16 fours and six sixes of his own) by No 4 Yuvraj Singh, and the cherry on the cake was a 32-ball 39 by skipper MS Dhoni.

The new-ball bowlers Zaheer Khan and Munaf Patel followed the act with early breakthroughs, and offie Harbhajan Singh was tough to score of. Not one bowler who turned his arm for India went wicket-less.

In the rival camp, the numbers were naturally a lot more more modest. The most economical of the lot was Andrew Flintoff, who gave away 6.7 runs per over. In the batting department, Pietersen's 63 and Ravi Bopara's 54 were two modest high-rises as compared to the sky scrapers on the Indian side of the fence.

After the warm-up game Mumbai, where England had been bowled out for 98, Pietersen had said the debacle didn't bother him. But after Rajkot, the visiting camp will have some serious thinking to do. "We'll sit down and see where we made a few mistakes," Pietersen said, without a hint of panic. "You've got to try to make sure you go over what you've done not so well and regroup. There's six games left in the series and we want to bring some real good cricket to Indore."

The visitors will have to take a U-turn in the next match on Monday to get back on the right path.

Heading: Bengal team accused of foul play - Indian Express
Content:
There were a couple of things that happened at the start of 34th over of India's innings that signalled the start of the final assault. The batting side had opted for the powerplays just as the umpires handed a cleaner, harder ball to England's bowlers.

But Yuvraj Singh, batting with a brace around his hips, his face screwed up in agony due to a back strain suffered a couple of overs back, didn't look like a man who could lead the carnage. Batting on 30 off 33 balls, and clearly in pain, even experts in the commentary box felt the left-hander should head back to the dressing room and leave the finishing touches to the big-hitters — Mahendra Singh Dhoni, Rohit Sharma and Yusuf Pathan — who were itching to get a piece of the action.

What followed was probably Yuvraj's most destructive innings ever — the kind that made the quality of bowling, field placements, pitch conditions or match situation seem irrelevant.

Anything outside the off-stump went flying over covers or scorched past point. Balls pitched on the legs usually plied two routes — those short of a length were flicked to the square leg fence, anything near a good length raced to, or over, mid-on.

In a nutshell, Yuvraj's 78-ball 138 with 16 fours and six sixes (not in one over, Stuart Broad would like to point out) was the kind of knock that could give the English bowlers nightmares over the duration of this series.

England captain Kevin Pietersen seemed as helpless at the post-match press conference as he did during the day. "Yuvraj played a fantastic innings. He was hitting the ball in a manner that most can't. At the end of the day, it's hard to lose, but there's little you can do if a batsman like Yuvraj plays an innings like he did," he said.

He might have been in pain on Tuesday, but the batsman's suffered through most of the year. His dismal run away in Australia and at home against South Africa meant he wasn't picked for the Tests in Sri Lanka. He got a big hundred in the warm-up game ahead of the one-dayers, but Ajantha Mendis gave him a torrid time once the serious business got underway.

He was left out of the Rest of India squad for the Irani Cup tie and it was back to the grind as he led the Board President XI against the visiting Aussies. Yuvraj did score a ton in that tour game, but the limelight was hogged by Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma.

Yuvraj himself called it his best innings to date. "It was important for me to find some form. I was not here to prove anything to anybody, but I did want to prove to myself that I belong in this league," he said.

Heading: IWHF orders probe into player’s accusation - Indian Express
Content:
In an alleged case of impersonation, Bengal played Ashrafuddin on the second day of the Under-22 CK Nayudu Trophy match against Tripura in the place of Bunty Gowala whose name had figured in the batting line-up on the previous day.

According to sources, after Asharafuddin had rolled his arm over on Friday, the official scorer brought the issue to the umpire's notice, and match referee, Sashi Nayar, from Jharkhand was called into action. Crying foul, the Tripura team management is learnt to have called up BCCI chief administrative officer Prof. Ratnakar Shetty, who reportedly suggested that the hosts play under a written protest. Tripura, instead, chose to play under a verbal protest.

While Bengal manager Saikat Goswami was tight-lipped on the issue, Cricket Association of Bengal (CAB) joint-secretary Arun Mitra said it was a minor mistake and the matter had been sorted out.

"It's Ashrafuddin who is playing, and not Gowala. Yesterday, Ashrafuddin batted, but his name was mistakenly written as Bunty Gowala in the list that was submitted to the scorer. We have clarified the same," he said.

Heading: Murray dumps Federer - Indian Express
Content:
A day after a junior national player accused a coach of misbehaving with her, the Indian Women's Hockey Federation (IWHF) on Friday ordered an inquiry into the allegations but claimed it was actually the girl herself who was at fault.

Chandigarh-based Navneet Kaur had accused goalkeeping coach A Edwards of making advances towards her at the ongoing national camp in Lucknow and said when she brought the matter to chief coach GS Bhangu's attention, she was ordered to leave the camp.

Stunned by the allegations, IWHF Secretary Amrit Bose said Navneet informed neither Bhangu nor the federation but said a probe has been ordered to get the real picture. "I don't know exactly what happened as everything was going smoothly till yesterday but it is an unpleasant episode in the history of Indian women's hockey. It is a gross violation of discipline and we are not going to tolerate this," Bose said.

"Both the player and goalkeeping coach have been asked to leave the camp. We are definitely going deep into the matter. I have asked for a detailed report from the chief coach at the earliest which will be put before the IWHF disciplinary committee," she added.

The IWHF secretary claimed that according to the initial report of the chief coach and other officials in the camp, it was Navneet who misbehaved with Edwards.

Bose also questioned Navneet's intention and said if the player had any such problem she should have straightaway approached her.

Heading: Export incentives for steel restored - Indian Express
Content:
Local derbies can often end up turning into drab encounters, with teams tending to suffer from the fear of losing, and preferring to defend. Even though Friday's I-League encounter between city giants Mahindra United and old warhorses Air-India at Cooperage provided a few moments of excitement in the latter period of play, the contest turned out to be a midfield tussle for a major part. The final score was 1-1.

The first half saw very few chances being created at either end, and the pace didn't seem to pick up till a few minutes before the half-time whistle. The Jeepmen forward line missed a decent chance to take the lead, and the teams went into the break locked at 0-0.

The teams seemed to come out with more energy in the second half, and in the 50th minute, Air-India, under new captain Chukwuma Odafia, almost took the lead. Striker Surojit Roy jumped for the ball inside the box and seemed to win it, but he also unfortunately got a piece of opposition goalkeeper Subhasish Chowdhury as it crept into the back of the net. The goal was disallowed by Goan referee Benjamin Silva.

Mahindra finally struck on a counterattack, and striker Sushil Kumar Singh put them in front in the 53rd minute. But that only served to motivate the airmen further, and Subhas Singh brought them right back into the game with a 68th minute equaliser. Air-India got another chance to snatch victory late in the game, but Ovieghara and striker Samson Singh failed to capitalise on a defensive error, and the chance went abegging.

Air-India coach Bimal Ghosh expressed disappointment at the standard of refereeing during the match, and believed that his team could have walked away with a win. "We missed a couple of chances in the first half and had a golden opportunity to steal it in the end. But I will not blame Ovieghara or Samson for that miss. These things happen in football," he said. If Surojit's goal would have been allowed, insisted Ghosh, the result could have been completely different as his team would have gone into the lead first.

Air-India now sit pretty at No 2 in the I-League table, having garnered 15 points from eight games.

Heading: Tatas, DoCoMo plan Rs 949-cr open offer - Indian Express
Content:
Fortune seems to be finally smiling on the country's beleaguered steel sector currently battling low prices and rising inventories, with the government tonight restoring the export incentives in the form of the Duty Entitlement Pass Book (DEPB) Scheme. What's more, the government is also likely to notify re-imposition of 10 per cent import duty this week.

"We have already written twice to the Finance Ministry to re-impose 10 per cent import duty on steel products in view of the domestic prices going down. The move is aimed at boosting the local utilities. We expect the notification this week," Steel Minister Ram Vilas Paswan said here. Steel Secretary Pramod Kumar Rastogi said earlier the Finance Ministry had sought certain clarifications on prices, which have already been furnished to it and hence the path has been cleared for the re-imposition of the said duty. With steel prices on a downward spiral, the producers had intensified their demand for re-imposition of the duty as well as imposition of 14 per cent Countervailing Excise Duty (CVED).

Coincidentally, the Commerce Ministry today restored DEPB benefits for steel makers shipping their produce to certain countries. In a notification, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) said the export incentives have been re-allowed in almost all steel products. The move is bound to enthuse the utilities, which were hitherto clamouring for restoration of DEPB benefits as they were incurring financial loss worth Rs 500 crores ever since its withdrawal. "The producers should be a happy lot," Rastogi said. The government had withdrawn the incentives in June primarily with a view to disincentivise exports to contain spiraling domestic prices of the alloy and bridge the widening its demand-supply mismatch, which was triggering discontentment among different industries. The erstwhile Indian Steel Alliance, the dissolved umbrella organization of the leading steel producers had earlier petitioned the government highlighting the plight of the utilities following withdrawal of incentives. But restoration of DEPB is unlikely to accrue much benefit to the producers as global steel prices have declined and as such there is not much reason to export. However, when prices pick up and demand spirals, exporting steel to the overseas could benefit the producers duly.

Paswan said strong domestic demand and consumption and well-managed economic fundamentals will enable India to ride out the economic crisis. "Well, there could be some problems with the Greenfield projects as they involve building projects from the scratch, but I do not see any reason on slowing of brownfield expansions, which are already on," he said. The minister ruled out any possibility of an economic package to bail out the utilities, saying things have not yet come to such a pass. Companies like Ispat and JSW have announced production cuts to offset shooting input costs and rising inventories. Director Tata Sons and former MD Tata Steel J J Irani has said that steel companies are in troubled times and they will have to manage their inventories well to maintain themselves.

Heading: Spectrum controversy in all its shades - Indian Express
Content:
After selling a 26 per cent stake in the parent company, Tata Teleservices Ltd and Tata Sons along with NTT DoCoMo of Japan will make an open offer to the shareholders of Tata Teleservices (Maharashtra) Ltd (TTML) for up to 20 per cent equity. The offer will be at a price of Rs 24.70 per share, costing around Rs 949 crore to the companies.

Announcing the details, Tata group chief Ratan Tata made it clear that "Our partnership with NTT DoCoMo is going to be a long-term partnership... for its technology, its value-added services and very high ethical standards and value systems."

The open offer price represents a premium of 22 per cent over TTML's Friday's closing of Rs 20.20 on the National Stock Exchange. The open offer will open on January 8 and close on January 27, 2009. The offer is for acquiring 38,42,41,919 shares or up to 20 per cent.

Japan's biggest mobile-phone operator NTT DoCoMo acquired a 26 per cent stake in Tata Teleservices Ltd (TTSL) for $2.7 billion (Rs 13,070 crore) on Wednesday. TTSL will issue fresh equity as part of the deal. The unlisted telecom is part of the sprawling Tata Group, and group firms own about 80 per cent of it. Temasek owns about 10 percent of the firm, while investor C Sivasankaran holds 8 per cent. "There is a plan to issue fresh equity. The details of it are being worked out," TTSL's managing director Anil Sardana said.

TTSL today said that it will roll out its GSM operations in January 2009. "It is a great pleasure and privilege for the Tata Group to partner with NTT DoCoMo. I hope to give the public a wider range of products and excellent bases of service not only in current technologies but in the technologies yet to come," Tata Sons chairman Ratan Tata said.

"The co-operation between DoCoMo and TTSL across marketing, handset development and technical support is expected to create new opportunities for both companies. We expect to earn more revenues from data services as it taps into the experience of its new stakeholder NTT DoCoMo.

We will bring in advanced value-added services which the Indian market has never seen before," Sardana said. About 11 per cent of TTSL's revenue comes from data.

Heading: RBI asks banks to review viability of 7 infra projects - Indian Express
Content:
The telcom sector in India is in a tangle because of a thickening controversy surrounding allocation of spectrum, the air waves on which data travel. As charges and counter-charges fly over government selling spectrum cheap, Rishi Raj splits the various hues and shades of the spectrum imbroglio:

•Why is it being alleged that communications minister A Raja granted licence and spectrum to a host of new players at throwaway prices, causing loss to the state exchequer?

It all began around middle of last year when the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) sough the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India's (Trai's) recommendation on whether the existing policy of having unlimited telecom players in a circle should be continued. DoT had also sought to know Trai's mind on a host of other issues like mergers and acquisitions, use of dual technology and roll-out obligations. While submitting its recommendations in August 2007, Trai said that the government should continue with the policy of no-capping with regard to entry of new players. It also said that 2G spectrum in 800, 900 and 1800 Mhz should not be auctioned while spectrum in all the other bands should be auctioned. As soon the recommendations were made public, a host of firms, mostly with no prior experience in telecom and some shell companies, submitted applications for telecom licences. Though the government accepted the Trai's recommendation of no-capping, seeing the deluge of applications it put a temporary bar by not accepting applications after October 1, 2007. Then, the DoT issued licences to only those firms, which had applied till September 25, 2007 and companies such as Swan, Unitech, Datacom, Loop Telecom, S Tel benefited from this. These companies have been granted/being granted spectrum on a circle basis.

•Was there anything wrong in this entire exercise?

The DoT granted these licences on a first-cum-first-served basis. As per the policy, alongwith a licence, the cost of an all-India licence is Rs 1,651 crore, while bundled spectrum of 4.4 Mhz is also given. The majority opinion was that since spectrum is a scarce resource, the government should not allot it bundled with licence but rather auction it to realize the market value. Recently, two companies, Swan and Unitech sold 45 per cent and 60 per cent stakes respectively to foreign players at valuations of around $2 billion. Since these two companies do not have network, subscribers or knowledge of telecom business, it is inferred that the huge valuation is the price of a paper called licence and spectrum, which are radio waves required to operate mobile services. Critics maintain that this money could have come to the government, which it let forgo by doling out licence and spectrum at a price discovered in 2001.

•What does Raja have to say?

Raja maintains that he has not done anything wrong. He went by the Trai recommendation of no-capping and not auctioning 2G spectrum. With regard to awarding licence at a price discovered in 2001, he says that the Trai did not ask for revising it, and the Cabinet had approved the price in 2003 so he was perfectly right in sticking to it. Regarding the stake sales by the two companies, Raja says that the deal is as per the corporate laws of the country and the new operators require funds to roll out network and services. As an afterthought he has proposed to bar promoters of new licensee firms from selling their equity till a period of three years.

•Is Raja right in his defence?

Yes and No. Yes, when he says that he went by Trai's recommendation on no-capping and not auctioning of 2G spectrum. No, because he later inflicted a temporary capping policy, which is still in force. Raja is wrong when he says that he went with Trai regarding the price of awarding new licences. Trai in 2003 had categorically said that all new licences should be awarded through a multi-stage bidding. Even the August 2007 recommendation said that a realistic price should be determined through a market mechanism.

•What's the difference between auctioning telecom licence and spectrum?

Historically, since the telecom sector was opened to the private operators in India, licences have been auctioned but spectrum has been bundled with it. However, companies pay a spectrum usage charge. If Raja would have auctioned the licence in the present case and given spectrum bundled with it, he would have been able to realize a market-determined price rather than a price discovered through auction in 2001. And the Trai recommendations did not stand in his way as far as auctioning of licence is concerned.

•Is there any other way these companies allegedly benefited through DoT?

Yes. A crucial recommendation of Trai with regard to mergers and acquisitions for new licensees was tweaked by the DoT, which led these companies to sell stakes. Trai had suggested that companies should not be eligible for mergers and acquisitions till they achieve their rollout obligations. Companies have to roll out networks covering 10 per cent of the circle by year one and 50 per cent by year three. However, DoT changed it and while it barred the companies for a total mergers and acquisitions till the end of year three, it allowed them to sell stakes up to 74 per cent before that. This helped Swan and Unitech to sell stakes even before they set up a single tower.

Heading: Union Bank to hire 5,000 workers by fiscal-end - Indian Express
Content:
In a significant one-time measure, the Reserve Bank of India has asked banks to undertake exclusive fresh financial viability study for seven major core sector projects in order to assess their eligibility for restructuring. These projects are likely to get further sops after the review.

These seven projects are Nandi Economic Corridor enterprises (Road Project and Township), GVK Industries (gas-based power project - phase II), Gautami Power Ltd (gas-based power project), Konaseema Gas Power (gas-based power project), New Tirupur Area Development Corporation (development of Tirupur area), Vemagiri Power Generation (gas-based power project) and Delhi Gurgaon Super Connectivity Ltd.

In case these projects are found eligible for restructuring and the banks concerned choose to undertake their restructuring, it has been decided, as a one-time measure, that the seven projects under implementation, would be categorised in 'standard' category even if the account was non-performing assets (NPA) provided such restructuring package is implemented within a period of six months. This move is in the wake of the current market developments, the RBI said.

The RBI said the banks have earlier represented that that there are occasions when the completion of infrastructure projects gets delayed for legal and other extraneous reasons.

Going by the existing norms for the infrastructure projects, financed by the banks/financial institutions after May 28, 2002, the date of completion of the project should be clearly spelt out at the time of financial closure of the project.

"In such cases, with effect from March 31, 2008, if the date of commencement of commercial production or operation extends beyond a period of two years after the date of completion of the infrastructure project, as originally envisaged at the time of initial financial closure of the project, the account should be treated as a substandard asset," the RBI said.

Heading: Credit growth non-inflationary, no need to worry, says Chidambaram - Indian Express
Content:
While global banks hit by the financial turmoil are going for a massive reduction in their employee base, for Indian banks it is now time to expand their human resources to undertake their expansion plans.

MV Nair, chairman and managing director, Union Bank of India, said the bank has plans to recruit 5,000 staff, including 4,000 at the officer level, by the end of the current fiscal. Earlier, State Bank of India, Bank of India and Bank of Baroda had announced similar plans to recruit more staffers to manage their growing operations. The additional staffers are necessary to manage the new branches the bank wants to open in the next few months. The bank has got the approval for the opening of 549 branches, including 10 specialised branches like industrial finance business and cash management services.

Talking to the media on the sidelines of the announcement of UBI's launch of the mobile banking facility 'U Mobile' in Mumbai on Friday, Nair said, "We got the approval from the RBI for the opening of 549 new branches just a week ago.:

Disclosing a host of other initiatives of his bank, Nair said the bank will have nearly 2,500 ATMs — as against the existing 1,500 — by the fiscal-end.

Heading: ‘The crisis should not be an excuse to go into a protectionist cocoon’ - Indian Express
Content:
Finance minister P Chidambaram today said there was no need to worry about high credit growth rate if it led to a non-inflationary economic growth. However, he said it was not possible to draw conclusions that credit flow to businesses was inadequate. Addressing mediapersons on board the Prime Minister's special aircraft, Chidambaram said, "I am not targeting any growth of credit. It is growing at 29 per cent today. If it is non-inflationary growth, we do not have to worry about it."

In fact, Chidambaram quoted former RBI governor Bimal Jalan who had said in an interview to The Indian Express earlier this week that there was no need to worry about high credit growth rates. "We have to juxtapose the rate of credit growth with inflation. If the growth is non-inflationary, then we can accept the current credit growth, but it depends upon its impact on inflation."

The minister later told The Indian Express that he is likely to get a report from public sector banks about how credit was distributed sector-wise in a couple of days. "We had asked banks to give us a fortnightly report on credit flow. There is concern that it is not reaching certain sectors. We need to get a clear picture," he said.

According to Chidambaram, it is, however, for the RBI governor to take a call on whether credit growth rate needs to be moderated or increased. In its review of the monetary policy on October 24, the RBI had said that the credit growth rate of 29 per cent till October 10 was well beyond the 20 per cent target set by it for the full year. It had let the event pass without any action to ease the monetary situation. But, subsequently, the RBI cut the CRR by 100 basis points to 5.5 per cent and the repo rate (the rate at which banks borrow from the RBI) by 50 basis points to 7.5 per cent.

When asked if another cut in CRR was coming, he said, it is for the RBI governor to answer. To a query that interest rates continued to be high in India despite the two rounds of repo rate cuts, Chidambaram said, the RBI Governor will respond as the situation develops.

Heading: Can’t have international regulation, says PM’s advisor - Indian Express
Content:
•Opening remarks on India's position at the Summit on Financial Markets and the World Economy.

FM: In his statement, the Prime Minister has highlighted three points he will make at the summit. The need for greater inclusivity, ensuring that the development prospects of developing countries do not suffer and the need to avoid protectionist tendencies. I have just returned from the G-20 Finance Minister's meeting and the G20 Finance Ministers have put out a communiqué.

The key point is, we must agree to a new order of global oversight. And this can come only by, as the Prime Minister said, greater inclusivity in the international financial system. In many ways, the IMF and the G-7 are too narrow and too small. A more inclusive system can provide better surveillance and serve as an early-warning mechanism.

The second is that while the world grapples with the crisis, the countries most hit by it find their growth prospects hampered. We must not forget that there are only a handful of economies that are driving the world economic growth. Among them are China and India. Resources must be made available to developing countries, including India, so that they can continue to grow and try to have economic development.

Third, the crisis should not be an excuse to go into a protectionist cocoon. That would be the worst way to solve the crisis. We must now try to encourage free flow of goods and services and must continue to enhance the flow of capital. Except for increasing free flow of goods, services and capital, there is no way in which the world will recover and get back to the growth path. All this requires deep thought... and quick agreement among the leaders.

•What about the global financial architecture that is being talked about?

FM: Among the things that we must agree on are common prudential and regulatory standards for all financial institutions in the world, especially those with global footprints. We must have convergence of accounting standards, we must agree to locate the resources and agree upon the channels through which this resource would be diverted to the developing countries, these could be the existing multinational institutions or we could devise an ad-hoc fund dispersing mechanism, and finally, the international institutions which constitute the global financial architecture must be reformed. And this goes beyond the IMF and World Bank. This includes the Bank for International Settlements and the Financial Stability Forum.

•Are we talking about a global regulator?

FM: See, the regulation in the present context is a function which national regulators will be loth to give up. That is why regulation must be national. If we can agree upon common prudential and regulatory standards, and then ask national regulators to apply those standards, there can be some kind of a global oversight, where the national regulators are doing their job. I don't think regulation can be raised to a global regulator. That's too ambitious, and perhaps not possible in today's circumstances.

•Does it mean there will be a global oversight body?

FM: I didn't use the word global oversight body. I just said there must be some way in which we can have global oversight through which commonly accepted regulatory and prudential standards are being applied by national regulators. But these things are to be talked over, these are ideas, these are positive things.

•The Prime Minister has talked about pump-priming the economy? But we have not seen any economic stimulus package so far.

FM: That's a question you should ask on the way back to India. We've just passed a supplementary demand, which is about Rs 1,05,000 crore additional cash expenditure. Where do you think it is going? All of it is going into NREG, rural development. Just look at the heads under which we have this.

•What would have happened if we had surveillance and early-warning mechanisms?

FM: In retrospective, it is clear that if there had been an effective surveillance mechanism, it could have or should have identified the huge risks that were being taken by some international financial entities. In the absence of this oversight mechanism, these financial entities, some of which have collapsed, took unacceptable risk. That was what led to the crisis in United States, which is there at the centre of the crisis.

•What will be the impact on India?

FM: We can't measure the impact. We have said, we will be indirectly impacted, there will be impact to some extent on our growth, our exports, and it will also impact the currency flows, as it has already. But we are confident that given the underlying strengths of Indian economy we can weather the crisis and still return a decent growth in 2008-09, even the IMF's last week's assessment places India's growth rate in the current fiscal at 7.8 per cent. We will still return a decent growth rate, we will suffer an indirect impact.

•Do we expect any serious outcomes given that the US has a lame-duck administration and India too is facing elections.

FM: The resolution of this crisis will take us to a point of time well beyond January 20, 2009. Likewise, it will take us to a point of time well beyond May 22, 2009, so I don't think we are going to take a election constricted point of view. We have to take a medium- to long-term point of view, and I believe the US also will take that view. So I think Obama inputs will be there in whatever President Bush presents. So we will have to take a view that takes us beyond those election dates. That is the stance that I think India will adopt.

Heading: US steps towards regulating esoteric instruments - Indian Express
Content:
The world turns its attention to the G-20 meeting at Washington DC this weekend, where the leaders of twenty developed and emerging economies will sit around a table to discuss the crisis in financial markets and try to arrive at some sort of consensus about how to minimise its impact. Where will the conference lead, according to the man advising the Indian PM? The main news is that there isn't going to be any thrust to formally internationalise financial regulation, as many in Europe, for example, want. "I don't think you can internationalise financial regulation," says Raghuram Rajan, the new honorary economic advisor to the prime minister. "What you can do is to strengthen forums where regulators exchange views, and allow independent bodies to comment on the quality of regulation in different countries." The flow and quality of information about how well financial firms are regulated will be the thrust of any international efforts, not an attempt at creating cross-border regulation of those firms.

It was widely expected that India would play a large role in shaping the consensus. And Rajan, recently brought in from the University of Chicago for his expertise on financial markets, would play a visible role. That doesn't seem to have worked out. It appears that Rajan, a professor at the University of Chicago's graduate school of business, won't be in the room when the discussions take place — won't even be in Washington DC. Rajan himself doesn't see this as a problem. He doesn't need to be there, evidently, because the Prime Minister has been well-prepared: he told The Indian Express in an e-mail exchange: "much of the work for these meetings is done beforehand — the meeting is often merely an airing of prepared statements."

His isn't the only absence that is causing comment. American president-elect Barack Obama's transition team has made it clear that Obama won't be attending the conference — and no member of his team, nor the candidates to be designated treasury secretary in his cabinet, is likely to be there. There is concern that this is self-defeating for the US, and Rajan agrees: "Obama is certainly the elephant who is not in the room." But it is clear what the pressures on Obama are, and that he sees this particular summit should be seen only as the first of many: "He would be clever to stay away since he cannot commit to anything just now, and will have the benefit of knowing what people want next time."

Re-opening trade talks, too, is something that has been called for. The Great Depression was marked by destructive tit-for-tat trade wars, and China's recent announcement of new export subsidies raised fears of something similar. Yes, agrees Rajan, the world needs to come out against that sort of thing: "We need more of a commitment to free trade, certainly a commitment to not go backwards." But is it likely that trade will go forwards? However beneficial, it is extremely unlikely politically, according to Rajan: "Concluding Doha would be a good thing, but there is little political capital to do so."

But the focus of the summit is expected to be the International Monetary Fund, which has made major changes to its style of operations recently, and is being looked to once again as the bulwark of financial stability. Does it have enough money? Gordon Brown thinks not. Rajan, once chief economist at the IMF, wants more money too. "If a large emerging market were to need money today, it could approach a hundred billion dollars or more," he says, pointing out that this is at least as much as the Russian government has spent stabilising their economy in the last month alone. Where will this come from? "The Fund needs to have new borrowing facilities of its own to be able to provide this." It may be guarantees — in other words, the IMF won't need to lay out all the money, merely underwrite other people —but "even if it is guarantees, there has to be the possibility of real money". What we then need to be concerned about is "the potential loss if someone defaults, and that loss will be shared by member countries." Thus reforming and restructuring the IMF to equitably share that loss is certainly going to be on the table.

Heading: ‘That’s what writers are digging deep for, that little bit of truth’ - Indian Express
Content:
As President George W Bush and other major world leaders gather in Washington for a summit to consider ways to battle the worst financial crisis since the 1930s, a presidential panel announced steps Friday to strengthen oversight of complex financial instruments partly blamed for the global financial crisis.

The action taken by the President's Working Group on Financial Markets is designed to bring more openness to the murky world of derivatives and credit default swaps — a type of corporate debt insurance — that played a role in the turmoil.

Under one move, the Federal Reserve, Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission agreed to exchange information on credit default swaps from private groups that will be set up to act as central clearinghouses for such transactions. That should help provide crucial information on the parties involved in the complex and unregulated products.

Credit default swaps, a roughly $60 trillion worldwide market, played a large role in the credit crisis that brought the downfall of Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., pushed giant insurer American International Group Inc. to the brink of bankruptcy, and forced Merrill Lynch & Co. to sell itself to Bank of America Corp. The swaps are commonly used contracts to insure against the default of financial instruments such as bonds and corporate debt. But they also are bought and sold as bets against bond defaults. Headed by Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson, the White House group includes Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke and Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Christopher Cox.

The White House group also called for public reporting of prices, trading volumes and other information on credit default swaps to "increase market transparency" for participants and the public. It also said regulators should have access to information about trades and positions on the investments for the purpose of "monitoring market trends, identifying potential issues, and preventing market manipulation and insider trading". The panel urged regulators in the US and overseas also should expand their efforts to share information.

Heading: Prachanda’s acid test - Indian Express
Content:
Nobel laureate Nadine Gordimer is arguably one of the greatest living writers in the English language. Anushree Majumdar caught up with her in New Delhi.

•You've been criticised, wrongly though, for the 'completeness' of your novels: the meticulous scene paintings and fully realised characters. Your attention to detail, nuance has been constant. Has this been a matter of choice or is good writing all about detail?

I must say I'm unaware of this criticism. But if we talk about detail, let's remember what your great R.K. Narayan said: he said that you have to look through the significant detail, and that's a lot of detail. Whether it's in a character or in a landscape, whatever it is. But to clutter the work with a whole lot of detail, I don't really do this so I don't know where this criticism comes from.

•I'm quoting you here. You've said, "To write as well as you can is the best way of serving your society, whether it's in conflict or whether it's post-conflict, if there is such a thing as post-conflict". How has South Africa's post-apartheid identity shaped your writing and your existence as a writer?

Whatever your circumstances as a writer, whether you're in the conflict, or whether the conflict is over or it hasn't come yet, two things are happening. You're changing all the time, in your perceptions of what human life is, and what human values are and the way humans behave. That comes from inside, you yourself are part of that. And from outside, you have the social pressures, school, family, friends, society, the profession or whatever you take up, and all around that, the laws in which you live, that control your moral values. So there are all these influences coming into the way you are dealing with the world imaginatively, through the use of the word, as your life goes on. In other words, when people talk about style, to me, no writer has a style. Because for myself, and for the writers whom I admire, what does for one book, is not going to be the voice you hear and in which you're going to tell the next story. Each time you move on in life and life moves on around you, you have to meet the challenge of new ways to use the word.

•While writing about apartheid and representing the broader anatomy of a diseased politics, you've often written about betrayal, personal as well as political. What compels you?

Because this is so much the big moral problem in our lives, in small things and in big things. In our love life, our sexual lives, in our relationship with our parents, with our children, with our friends, there are so many forms of betrayal. I think this is for me, this is the moral touchstone. What have I done there, which was indeed a betrayal of the way I think my attitude should be to you. Whether it is in social, personal or political life. Whether you go to cast your vote, if there has been a split in the party that you follow, if you vote on this side, are you not betraying the other side and vice versa. To me, the problems of human existence indeed, is that we're all subject to betrayal. Even of ourselves sometimes. We don't do what we would have liked ourselves to have done, or have thought what we should have thought.

•Your identity as a writer as well as an activist must be pressurizing: people tend to demand "action" from you, as it was recently witnessed when you visited Israel. How do you react to this?

In South Africa, there was objection from people who are very naturally in favour of justice for the Palestinians, which I am too. They objected to my going to Israel, but I also went to Palestine and I was welcomed by the Palestinians, because they know I believe that there should be justice for them, and I cannot accept Hamas' idea that Israel should not exist, that they should be pushed into the sea. And again, you have to find some way, and unfortunately, it's such a tiny piece of land, they've been there since ancient times and you've got to find some way.

When I was in Israel, I aroused some strong feelings because I said the occupational areas which I saw, I think are absolutely wrong. In some cases, they've gone on building there. My friends there, including my friend, the writer Amos Oz, he started Peace Now, he gets into hot water and is despised by the fundamentalists there. His view is the same, that they must get out of these occupied sites.

In other words, here again is the question of betrayal. I stick by my reasons for going there and I faced the opposition on both sides. I happen to know the great conductor and pianist Daniel Barenboim, he's got an orchestra as you know, with Israelis and Palentinians, that he takes all around the world. I said, Daniel, I'm being shot at from all sides, and he said, Nadine, either don't go or just accept that you will be shot at from all sides. So I went and I don't regret it.

It was interesting, the attitude of my comrades, from the ANC. One or two said that you must not go, and others, people of indeed, really high up in the movement said Go. Look what we did here, we had to sit down at the table with Mr. De Klerk, we had to sit down with these murderers, and work out that we were not going to have a terrible civil war, that we would somehow put together a government of national unity, recognize that each side had to give up some of their ideals. Of course this seems to be impossible between the Israelis and the Palestinians. As soon as one side agrees, the other side says no.

•You're an atheist. Would you say that if there has to be a religion, then it must be Truth? Your work deals so much with internal motives and you're always digging deeper, it's always the truth you seek.

Indeed, it is. And I would apply to that to all writers, the ones who are really worthy of the name. And I say this very humbly on part of all of us, because we can only find as we go down and down, below the surface, below the facts, below the commentary of all the facts, below what you see on television and you go into all the factors that make up the moment. The shocking image you see on television, what happened to those people before they brought them there, what happens to them afterwards? And this is not a matter of analysis, it's what happens inside people. And I think in the case of apartheid, writers and playwrights, some of us who have had the good fortune to be read outside, we moved the freedom movement along, because we made the world understand what this concept of apartheid is, this concept of racism, whether it is about colour or religion, what it does to the human being, how it distorts human nature. And I think that's what writers are digging deep into, that little bit of truth, that in all humility, we are able to dredge up.

•You've said that The White Tiger by Aravind Adiga is "brilliantly written" but he "rubbed it in too much". Where should a writer stop, check himself, so that it does not affect the storytelling?

I don't give any direction to any other author. I'm looking at it as a reader and he's quite right. We shouldn't censor ourselves on the daily obscenities that we use, and the way we use as insults, different parts of our bodies, male and female, whatever. Because this is what we do in our daily lives. But sometimes, I felt, the same thing was emphasized twice. But this is really a small criticism; I still think it's a remarkable book. And for a novelist, it's a brilliant first novel. But one must say what one thinks, I just thought there was too much of a nudge. "This is something obscene now, listen to me" or "Just listen to what I'm going to say" but I get it anyway, you get it anyway.

And that's how words lose their meaning. We all say "Fucking this and fucking that", but it has no pejorative meaning anymore. We used to say "Bloody hell" and then we began to say "Fucking this"—it's all beginning to lose its force. We'll have to have a new obscenity. Perhaps you've got some in your language.

•You have a wonderful relationship with the short story form, in spite of your novels, you keep coming back to it every couple of years.

It's a wonderful form and it's not an easy form to use and it's closer to poetry than is the novel. People ask how do you know whether it's going to be a short story or a novel? To me, a short story is like an egg, it's complete. There's a shell, there's a white, there's the yoke, with the beginning of life in there. And it comes to me complete like that, I know exactly how it begins and how it ends, and I write it straight off. With a novel, it's a kind of journey, it goes in stages, I know that I'm starting here, and I know the end. But the stages in between as I write, I've got it marked out in my head, but sometimes, the necessity comes that other characters come in, that I hadn't visualised. But the main characters, the beginning and the end, the theme is always there. Because for me, there are two things in a novel: there's a theme, and there is the narration and the characters which carry the theme.

•Have you ever felt that the online "revolution" of reading as well as writing might take over the Book?

I've been speaking against that phenomenon. The book indeed, you can take anywhere with you, you don't require a battery, you don't require any sort of gadget, you don't require an electrical unit. There isn't anywhere that you can't take it.

All the other things we have, the internet and so on, is great for information. But communication at the deeper level, you can do that with a book. When you want to pick up the book again and just turn back to page 52, because did you really understand all that was there? With a machine, you've got to work it out, you've got to press buttons and things and work it up. That's why, for information, the new technology is wonderful. But it cannot replace, as I fear it will, the printed written word. I see it happening, nowadays, books are going on to your mobile. There's been one case, some American, calls himself a writer, actually wrote a book for this, not to be printed at all. I think it's a tremendous loss.

I always give the same example because I find it so striking: I'm sure you were told a bedtime story. And you began to connect the words with what you looked at, began to learn to read before you even went to school. Words came together, the written word and the spoken word. Now the kid is put in front of the TV and the bedtime story is gone.

I have a granddaughter in France, my daughter married a Frenchman years ago. She has a little boy. They came to South Africa, he's very intelligent and played around and was full of curiosity about everything. We live far from the sea, we took a trip to the sea. I remember my childhood and all children I've seen, the joy of digging in the sand and digging up the crabs, building sandcastles. He took out of his pocket a videogame and he sat on this beautiful beach with all the things to play with and the little fish to try and catch, and he played a videogame. I said to my granddaughter "For God's sake, he might as well be shut in a room somewhere. Why do you allow this?" But he won't go anywhere without it. He's a very intelligent kid and I thought what a shame. He's cutting himself off from nature and activity. You could take a book to the sea but you'll put it down in favour of the image in front of you, it is the image that captures you.

I'm going now to Mexico for the 80th birthday of the great writer Carlos Fuentes, he's asked me to be there and speak. I have to give an address there; it's on the subject The Image and the Word, the rivalry between them at present.

•Which is the last Indian book you read and what did you think about it?

Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger. Also, I read Amitav Ghosh's The Sea of Poppies, most impressive. But I always go back to Tagore, Narayan. At home, in the Indian diplomatic office, Vikas Swarup, his book Q & A! That's a really interesting book and I hear that there's a movie out as well.

•What has been the most defining moment in this visit to India?

It's been a good time because I have met a lot of fellow writers, there's been a lot of exchange, which I didn't have when I came the last time for the Nehru lecture in Delhi. So that's been important. Some of them are quite surprised that I read a lot of Indian writing.
